items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Most cities that launched door-to-door vaccination drives in the 2010s saw only modest gains in childhood immunization rates. Riverton, a mid-sized port city, was a striking exception to that pattern. ______ its rate climbed from 71 percent to 94 percent in just two years, a jump larger than that recorded by any other participating city.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence before the blank says Riverton was an exception to the pattern of modest gains. The sentence after it backs up that same claim with vivid evidence: a 23-point jump, bigger than any other city's. Because sentence two confirms and strengthens sentence one, 'Indeed' is the right transition.

A.why: You saw a contrast between Riverton's big jump and the modest gains elsewhere, and you let that surface contrast drive your choice. But the sentence right before the blank already says Riverton was an exception. The jump confirms that claim instead of turning against it.

C.why: You treated the rise in the rate as one example drawn from a larger group. The rise isn't a sample of several exceptions. It is the evidence for the one exception already named, so it confirms the point rather than illustrating it.

D.why: You read a cause-and-effect link that isn't there. Being an exception didn't cause Riverton's rate to climb. The climb is the reason Riverton counts as an exception.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Astronomers value the planned Halvorsen Array for two separate capabilities. First, its twelve dishes can be linked electronically to act as a single telescope with extraordinary resolution. ______ the array can observe in several radio frequencies at once, allowing researchers to follow fast-changing sources such as pulsars without switching instruments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says there are two capabilities, and the second sentence gives the first one. The sentence after the blank gives the second: a new item of the same kind. An addition word is needed, so 'In addition' is correct.

B.why: You assumed the first capability produces the second. Linking dishes for resolution doesn't cause the array to observe in several frequencies at once. The two are independent features.

C.why: You read the second capability as replacing the first. The passage says astronomers value both, so nothing is being swapped out.

D.why: You mixed up reinforcing a point with adding one. 'In other words' would mean sentence two restates the resolution feature, but it describes a completely different capability, the second of the two.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Nutritionist Ama Owusu argues that the fiber in whole lentils sharply slows the rate at which sugars from a meal enter the bloodstream. Her 2021 feeding trial offers strong support for that view. ______ participants who ate a lentil side dish with white rice showed blood-glucose peaks nearly 30 percent lower than those of participants who ate the rice alone, and the effect lasted well into the afternoon.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence before the blank says the trial strongly supports Owusu's view. The sentence after it gives the striking result that shows how strong that support is. Because sentence two confirms and intensifies sentence one, 'Indeed' is the most logical choice.

A.why: You took the comparison between the two groups of participants as a contrast between the sentences. The lower peaks agree with the claim that the trial supports Owusu, so a word that pushes back doesn't fit.

B.why: 'Similarly' needs a second, parallel case that resembles the first. The glucose result isn't a separate case like the trial. It is the trial's own finding, so it reinforces the point rather than comparing it to something else.

D.why: You read the result as replacing something in the sentence before. Nothing is rejected or swapped out. The result supports exactly what came before.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Cover crops such as rye and clover, planted between growing seasons, benefit farms in several distinct ways. Their dense roots hold soil in place during winter storms, greatly reducing erosion. ______ when the plants are cut down in spring, they decompose into organic matter that helps the soil retain water through the dry summer months.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says cover crops help in several ways. The second gives one benefit, erosion control, and the sentence after the blank gives another, water retention. A second, parallel item calls for an addition word, so 'Moreover' is correct.

A.why: You read the water-retention benefit as an example of the sentence right before the blank. It isn't a case of erosion control. It is a separate benefit, another member of the 'several ways'.

B.why: You sensed a shift, from winter to spring and from roots to decomposition, and read it as a contrast. Both sentences describe benefits pointing the same direction, so nothing is being conceded or reversed.

C.why: You assumed the erosion control causes the water retention. The decaying plant matter helps the soil hold water whether or not the roots prevented erosion. The two benefits are parallel, not cause and effect.

items.stimulus: Folklorists who study the Appalachian 'Jack tales' note that the stories served more than one purpose for the families who told them. They entertained children during long winter evenings, when farm work slowed and households gathered by the fire. ______ the tales handed down practical lessons, since Jack's success usually depended on patience, thrift, and a sharp eye for a stranger's intentions.

items.explanation: The first sentence says the tales served more than one purpose. The second names entertainment, and the sentence after the blank names a different purpose, teaching practical lessons. A new item of the same kind calls for 'Additionally'.

D.why: You assumed the lessons follow from the entertainment. The passage doesn't say the tales taught lessons because they were entertaining. It lists the two purposes side by side.

C.why: 'Likewise' needs a second creature or behavior that resembles the first. The second sentence describes the same wrasses and the same boldness, so it reinforces the point rather than drawing a comparison.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Seismologist Rena Okafor has spent a decade monitoring the Tarsin Fault, which typically releases strain through thousands of tremors too faint for nearby residents to feel. The magnitude 6.1 earthquake that struck the fault in 2019 was therefore a striking departure from its usual behavior. ______ in the forty years of records preceding that event, no tremor on the fault had exceeded magnitude 3.5.

items.explanation: The sentence before the blank says the 2019 quake was a striking departure from the fault's usual behavior. The sentence after it backs up that claim: for forty years nothing larger than magnitude 3.5 had happened, which is exactly why a 6.1 counts as an outlier. The second sentence strengthens the first rather than adding a separate point, so you need an emphasis word. 'Indeed' is that word.

C.why: You treated the second sentence as a result of the first. The forty quiet years came before the 2019 quake, so they can't be its consequence. They are evidence for calling it a departure.

D.why: 'Instead' means one thing is taking the place of another. Nothing is being replaced here. The second sentence confirms the first.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Before a revised coastal chart is released, cartographers at the national hydrographic office check it against three independent sources. They start by comparing every depth figure on the draft with the most recent sonar surveys of the seabed. ______ they cross-reference each lighthouse, buoy, and beacon against the coast guard's current registry of navigational aids. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The passage describes three separate checks, and the words 'start by' and 'Lastly' mark the first and third. The sentence after the blank gives the second check, which is a new item of the same kind as the first. That is simple addition, so 'In addition' is correct.

A.why: You noticed the umbrella phrase 'three independent sources' and expected an example. But the sentence just before the blank is already one specific check. The registry check isn't an instance of the sonar comparison. It is a separate check that comes next.

B.why: 'Even so' introduces something that goes against what came before. The registry check doesn't undercut the sonar comparison. It is simply the next step in the same procedure.

D.why: You read the second check as a result of the first. Checking depth figures doesn't lead to checking lighthouses and buoys. The two are independent steps in a planned sequence.

items.stimulus: To slow drivers on Harlow Avenue, traffic engineer Lucía Brandt recommended that the city narrow the street from four lanes to two and widen its sidewalks. B.why: 'Otherwise' introduces what would happen if something else were not true. The plaza vote isn't a hypothetical alternative. It is what the council actually did.

C.why: 'For instance' introduces one example drawn from a larger group. The passage doesn't set up a group of actions to sample from. The plaza vote is the single action that shows how far the council went.

per_choice.D: 'Instead' means the second benefit replaces the first. The erosion benefit still holds. The fertilizer savings add to it.

items.subtype_name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
items.stimulus: Astronomers have generally expected comets to lose most of their surface ice after a few hundred passes near the Sun, fading into dim, inactive bodies. Comet Halvorsen-4, however, remains unusually active even though it has completed thousands of such orbits. ______ when it swung past the Sun last spring, its glowing coma outshone that of every other comet observed that year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence before the blank says Halvorsen-4 is still unusually active. The sentence after it gives vivid support: its coma outshone every other comet that year. This strengthens the same claim instead of adding a new one or reversing it, so 'Indeed' is correct.

A.why: The passage already contains 'however' and 'even though', so you expected another reversal. But the bright coma doesn't go against the comet's unusual activity. It confirms it. The contrast with general expectations is already dealt with in the sentence before the blank.

B.why: 'Alternatively' offers another possibility. The bright coma isn't a competing explanation or option. It is evidence for the claim just made.

C.why: You compared the bright coma with the 'dim, inactive bodies' mentioned earlier. The sentence before the blank already says Halvorsen-4 is the exception. The coma supports that point rather than contrasting with it.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: In a three-year study of upland meadows, ecologist Moira Lindqvist compared plots heavily browsed by red deer with plots where browsing was light. Where deer were abundant, they stripped away the low shrubs that ground-nesting birds such as meadow pipits use to conceal their nests, and pipit nesting success fell sharply. Nuthatches and tits nesting in tree cavities at the plot edges, however, fared equally well under both conditions. Lindqvist's results suggest that fencing deer out of a heavily browsed meadow would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: increase nesting success among ground-nesting birds but have little effect on cavity-nesting birds.
increase nesting success among cavity-nesting birds but have little effect on ground-nesting birds.
decrease nesting success among ground-nesting birds but have little effect on cavity-nesting birds.
increase nesting success among both ground-nesting birds and cavity-nesting birds.
items.explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: heavy browsing → shrubs lost → ground-nester success falls, while cavity nesters are unaffected. Fencing deer out reverses the condition, so the shrubs and their cover should return. The group that was harmed, ground nesters, should recover, and cavity nesters, who were never affected, should show little change.

B.why: You got the direction right but attached it to the wrong group. The passage says cavity nesters fared the same under both conditions. Ground nesters were the ones that depended on shrub cover.

C.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Browsing lowered pipit success, so removing the browsing should raise it, not lower it further.

D.why: You assumed that what helps one group helps every group. Cavity nesters showed no response to browsing, so nothing in the passage supports a gain for them.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Many public health officials have assumed that a tax on sugary drinks reduces consumption about equally across a population. A study of one midsize city's two-cent-per-ounce soda tax complicates that view. After the tax took effect, soda purchases fell substantially in low-income households, for which the price increase was a noticeable share of grocery spending, but barely changed in high-income households. The study's findings suggest that if the city repealed the tax, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: purchases in high-income households would likely rise, while those in low-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income households would likely rise, while those in high-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income households would likely fall further, while those in high-income households would change little.
purchases in low-income and high-income households would likely rise by roughly similar amounts.
items.explanation: The finding: tax → purchases fall in low-income households, with little change in high-income ones. Repealing the tax removes the price increase. The group that responded, low-income households, would likely buy more again, and the group that barely responded would likely stay about the same.

A.why: You swapped the groups. High-income purchases barely moved when the tax arrived, so there is little reason to expect them to move when it leaves.

C.why: You kept the right group but missed that repeal reverses the change. Taking away the price increase should push purchases back up, not down.

D.why: You fell back on the popular view the passage sets up only to undercut. The study found the two groups responded very differently, so an equal response to repeal isn't supported.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Ceramic coatings are widely applied to turbine blades on the assumption that they reduce wear at any operating temperature. Materials engineer Tomas Okafor found otherwise. Above about 600°C, his coating fused into a hard, glassy layer, and coated blades wore far more slowly than uncoated ones. Below that temperature, the coating remained powdery, and coated and uncoated blades wore at the same rate. Okafor's results suggest that in an engine redesigned so that its blades run at 450°C instead of 700°C, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: coated blades would likely wear more slowly than uncoated blades.
coated and uncoated blades would likely wear at about the same rate.
coated blades would likely wear faster than uncoated blades.
coated blades would likely wear even more slowly than at 700°C.
items.explanation: The finding splits at 600°C. Above it, the coating forms a glassy layer and slows wear. Below it, the coating stays powdery and gives no advantage. At 450°C the redesigned engine is below the threshold, so coated and uncoated blades should wear at about the same rate.

A.why: You applied the high-temperature result to a low-temperature case. A wear advantage appears only above 600°C, and 450°C falls in the half of the finding where it disappears.

C.why: You overshot the change. Below 600°C the passage reports equal wear, not faster wear for coated blades. Losing an advantage is not the same as gaining a disadvantage.

D.why: You added an assumption the passage doesn't contain: that cooler running improves the coating's performance. The passage says that below 600°C the coating does nothing to reduce wear.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Many marine larvae drift for weeks before choosing a place to settle. Marine biologist Keiko Arashiro played underwater recordings in tanks and found that oyster larvae settled in far greater numbers near speakers broadcasting the crackling sounds of a healthy reef than near silent speakers. Mussel larvae, by contrast, settled at the same rate whether or not reef sounds were playing. Arashiro's findings suggest that if speakers playing healthy-reef recordings were installed on a degraded, quiet reef, ______

oyster larvae would likely settle there in smaller numbers, while mussel settlement would change little.
oyster larvae and mussel larvae would both likely settle there in noticeably greater numbers.
oyster larvae would likely settle there in greater numbers, while mussel settlement would change little.
items.explanation: The finding: reef sound → more oyster settlement, with no effect on mussels. Adding reef sound to a quiet reef applies that condition, so oyster settlement should rise and mussel settlement should stay about the same.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Cartographers often add shaded relief (simulated shadows that make hills appear three-dimensional) on the assumption that it helps every reader judge terrain. A study by geographer Lena Fairweather tested that assumption. Novice map readers judged the relative elevation of points far more accurately on maps with shaded relief than on maps without it, whereas experienced readers, who infer elevation from contour lines, performed equally well on both. Fairweather's results suggest that removing the shaded relief from a hiking map would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: reduce experienced readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving novices' largely unchanged.
improve novice readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving experienced readers' largely unchanged.
reduce novice readers' accuracy in judging elevation while leaving experienced readers' largely unchanged.
reduce novice and experienced readers' accuracy in judging elevation by similar amounts.
items.explanation: The finding: shaded relief → better elevation judgments for novices, with no difference for experienced readers. Removing it takes away the aid, so novices should become less accurate. Experienced readers, who rely on contour lines, should be largely unaffected.

B.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Novices did better with shading, so taking it away should lower their accuracy, not raise it.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Chloride from road salt seeps into concrete bridge decks and rusts the steel reinforcing bars inside. In a ten-year field study, civil engineer Rosa Delacroix found that heavy salting sharply accelerated rebar corrosion in decks made of ordinary concrete. In decks sealed with a waterproof membrane beneath the pavement, however, corrosion proceeded at the same slow rate seen in unsalted ordinary decks, whether the road above was salted or not. Delacroix's findings imply that where winter roads are heavily salted, a deck built with the membrane would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: corrode faster than an otherwise identical deck built without a membrane.
corrode at about the same rate as an otherwise identical deck without one.
corrode more slowly than an otherwise identical deck built without a membrane.
show no corrosion at all, unlike an otherwise identical deck without one.
items.explanation: Under heavy salting, the ordinary deck's corrosion is sharply accelerated, while the membrane deck stays at the slow, unsalted rate. Comparing the two under the same salted conditions, the membrane deck should corrode more slowly.

B.why: You ignored the condition the question names. The two decks corrode at similar rates only without salt. With heavy salting, the ordinary deck speeds up and the membrane deck doesn't.

D.why: You read 'no effect from salt' as 'no corrosion.' The passage says membrane decks still corroded, just at a slow rate.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: It is often claimed that eighteenth-century musicians simply favored slower tempos than modern performers do. Musicologist Anika Brandt argues instead that the room mattered. Comparing tempo markings that composers revised when works moved between venues, she found that in highly reverberant churches, fast passages were marked noticeably slower, probably so that rapid notes would not blur in the echo. Slow movements, however, kept their original markings. Brandt's findings suggest that if a lively dance movement written for a small salon were moved to a cathedral, it would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: be marked at a slower tempo, while a slow movement moved along with it would keep its marking.
keep its marking, while a slow movement moved along with it would be marked at a slower tempo.
be marked at a faster tempo, while a slow movement moved along with it would keep its marking.
be marked at a slower tempo, and a slow movement moved along with it would be slowed as well.
items.explanation: The finding: reverberant venue → fast passages marked slower, while slow movements stay unchanged. A lively dance moving into a cathedral meets exactly that condition, so it should be slowed. A slow movement on the same program would keep its marking.

B.why: You swapped which kind of movement changes. Brandt found that fast passages were slowed and slow movements were left alone.

C.why: You picked the right movement but the wrong direction. Echo blurs rapid notes, so composers slowed fast passages rather than speeding them up.

D.why: You extended the slowdown to every movement, which is the popular view Brandt argues against. The passage says slow movements kept their original markings.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Etchers have long dampened paper before printing, believing that moist paper picks up ink better from every part of a plate. Conservator Ilse Marchetti tested that practice. On dampened paper, ink transferred far more completely from deeply bitten lines than it did on dry paper, but shallow, lightly bitten lines printed equally well on both. Marchetti's results suggest that if an etcher who had always used dampened paper switched to dry paper, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the shallow lines would likely print less fully, while the deep lines would print about as well as before.
the deep lines would likely print more fully, while the shallow lines would print about as well as before.
both the deep lines and the shallow lines would likely print noticeably less fully than before.
the deep lines would likely print less fully, while the shallow lines would print about as well as before.
items.explanation: The finding: dampening → fuller ink transfer from deep lines, with no difference for shallow lines. Switching to dry paper removes that benefit, so the deep lines should print less fully and the shallow lines should look about the same as before.

A.why: You swapped the line types. Shallow lines printed equally well on dry and damp paper. Only the deep lines depended on dampening.

B.why: You picked the right line type but the wrong direction. Dampening helped deep lines, so dropping it should make them print less fully, not more.

C.why: You accepted the traditional belief that the passage sets up to test. Marchetti found that shallow lines were unaffected by dampening, so they shouldn't get worse on dry paper.

items.subtype_name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
items.stimulus: On a regional map, a circular boundary with center $O$ has a radius of $6$ centimeters. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on the boundary, and minor arc $AB$ has a length of $5\pi$ centimeters.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of central angle $AOB$?
items.explanation: The circumference is $2\pi(6) = 12\pi$ cm. Arc $AB$ is $\frac{5\pi}{12\pi} = \frac{5}{12}$ of the circle, so the central angle is $\frac{5}{12}(360°) = 150°$.

A.why: You used the diameter, $12$, where the radius belongs. That gave a circumference of $24\pi$ and a fraction of $\frac{5}{24}$, which is half the real one.

C.why: You found the central angle of the major arc, $360° - 150°$. The question is about minor arc $AB$.

D.why: You took the circumference to be $\pi r = 6\pi$ instead of $2\pi r$. That doubled the fraction to $\frac{5}{6}$.

items.subtype_name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
items.stimulus: A city is redesigning a circular plaza with an area of $1{,}600\pi$ square meters. A curved path will run along the plaza's edge from one entrance to another, and the path spans a central angle of $135°$.
items.stem: What is the length, in meters, of the curved path?

C.why: You divided the angle by $180$ instead of $360$, so you took $\frac{3}{4}$ of the circumference. That is twice the correct length.

D.why: You took $\frac{3}{8}$ of the plaza's area, which gives the area of the sector, not the length of the arc.

items.subtype_name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
items.stimulus: Marine biologists tracking a tagged dolphin found that it swam along part of a circular ring of buoys around a reef. The ring has a radius of $15$ meters, and the dolphin covered an arc of length $12\pi$ meters along the ring.
items.stem: What is the measure, in radians, of the central angle of the arc the dolphin swam?

D.why: You found $2\pi - \frac{4\pi}{5}$, which is the angle of the part of the ring the dolphin did not swim.

items.subtype_name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
items.stimulus: In a sports science trial, an athlete runs counterclockwise around a circular track with a radius of $30$ meters, starting at a marked point. A sensor shows that the athlete stopped after running a total distance of $200\pi$ meters.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle of the arc the athlete covered after completing the last full lap?
items.explanation: One lap is $2\pi(30) = 60\pi$ m. Since $\frac{200\pi}{60\pi} = 3\frac{1}{3}$, the athlete ran $3$ full laps plus $\frac{1}{3}$ of a lap. That last part has a central angle of $\frac{1}{3}(360°) = 120°$.

A.why: You correctly found the leftover $\frac{1}{3}$ lap, but you multiplied it by $180°$ instead of $360°$.

C.why: You used $60$, the diameter, as the radius. That gave a lap of $120\pi$ m, so you found $1\frac{2}{3}$ laps and a leftover angle of $240°$.

D.why: $1{,}200°$ is the total angle for all $3\frac{1}{3}$ laps. You still need to remove the full laps and keep only the part after the last one.

items.subtype_name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
items.stimulus: A seismologist models Earth's surface as a circle with a radius of $6{,}400$ kilometers. Along the shorter arc of that circle, a monitoring station is $1{,}600\pi$ kilometers from an earthquake's epicenter.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of the central angle between the epicenter and the station?
items.explanation: The circumference is $2\pi(6{,}400) = 12{,}800\pi$ km. The arc is $\frac{1{,}600\pi}{12{,}800\pi} = \frac{1}{8}$ of the circle, so the central angle is $\frac{1}{8}(360°) = 45°$.

A.why: You treated $6{,}400$ as the diameter's half twice over, using $12{,}800$ as the radius. That doubled the circumference and halved the angle.

C.why: You used $\pi r$ for the circumference instead of $2\pi r$. That doubled the fraction to $\frac{1}{4}$.

D.why: You found the central angle of the longer arc, $360° - 45°$. The distance given is measured along the shorter arc.

items.subtype_name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
items.stimulus: A folklore studies team records a village custom built around a "fairy ring," a circle of mushrooms with a radius of $9$ meters. In the custom, a dancer walks along the ring through a central angle of $\frac{7\pi}{6}$ radians before stopping.
items.stem: What is the length, in meters, of the arc the dancer walks?
items.explanation: With the angle in radians, arc length is $s = r\theta = 9 \cdot \frac{7\pi}{6} = \frac{21\pi}{2}$ meters. As a check, $\frac{7\pi/6}{2\pi} = \frac{7}{12}$ of the circumference $18\pi$ is also $\frac{21\pi}{2}$.

A.why: You used $2\pi - \frac{7\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}$, which is the part of the ring the dancer does not walk.

C.why: You multiplied the angle by the diameter, $18$, instead of the radius, $9$, so your answer is twice the arc length.

D.why: You computed $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, which is the area of the sector, not the length of its arc.

items.subtype_name: Solve a given system, where one variable is already isolated
items.stimulus:
An urban planning student checks this system from a zoning worksheet.

$y = 3x$

$x + y = 20$
items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. What is the value of $y$?
items.explanation: The first equation already gives $y$ in terms of $x$. Substitute $3x$ for $y$ in the second equation: $x + 3x = 20$, so $4x = 20$ and $x = 5$. Then put this back into $y = 3x$ to get $y = 3(5) = 15$.

A.why: You solved for $x = 5$ correctly and then stopped. The question asks for $y$, so you still need to substitute back into $y = 3x$.

B.why: You combined $x + 3x$ as $2x$, which gives $x = 10$. The two terms add to $4x$.

D.why: $20$ is the value of $x + y$ given in the second equation. It is not the value of $y$ alone.

items.subtype_name: Solve a given system, where one variable is already isolated
items.stimulus:
A marine biology student uses this system in a lab exercise.

$x = 2y - 1$

$3x + y = 32$
items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Substitute $2y - 1$ for $x$ in the second equation: $3(2y - 1) + y = 32$, so $6y - 3 + y = 32$, $7y = 35$ and $y = 5$. Then $x = 2(5) - 1 = 9$.

A.why: $5$ is the value of $y$, the first variable you find. The question asks for $x$, so substitute $y = 5$ into $x = 2y - 1$.

C.why: You dropped the coefficient 3 and wrote $(2y - 1) + y = 32$, which gives $y = 11$ and $x = 21$.

D.why: $35$ is the value of $7y$ partway through the work. You still need to divide by 7 and then substitute back to find $x$.

items.subtype_name: Solve a given system, where one variable is already isolated
items.stimulus:
An archaeology student sets up this system while cataloguing a site.

$y = x + 4$

$2x + y = 19$
items.stem: What is the solution $(x, y)$ to the given system of equations?
items.explanation: Substitute $x + 4$ for $y$ in the second equation: $2x + x + 4 = 19$, so $3x = 15$ and $x = 5$. Then $y = 5 + 4 = 9$. The pair $(5, 9)$ satisfies both equations.

A.why: $(3, 7)$ satisfies $y = x + 4$, but $2(3) + 7 = 13$, not $19$. Check that a pair works in both equations.

C.why: $(7, 5)$ satisfies $2x + y = 19$, but $5 \neq 7 + 4$. It fails the first equation.

D.why: You found the right values but swapped them. The ordered pair lists $x$ first, and $x = 5$.

items.subtype_name: Solve a given system, where one variable is already isolated
items.stimulus:
A folklore studies student sets up this system for a coding exercise.

$y = -2x$

$5x - y = 21$
items.stem: The solution to the given system of equations is $(x, y)$. What is the value of $y$?
items.explanation: Substitute $-2x$ for $y$ in the second equation: $5x - (-2x) = 21$, so $7x = 21$ and $x = 3$. Then $y = -2(3) = -6$.

A.why: You treated $5x - (-2x)$ as $3x$, which gives $x = 7$ and $y = -14$. Subtracting a negative adds, so the result is $7x$.

C.why: $3$ is the value of $x$. The question asks for $y$, so substitute back into $y = -2x$.

D.why: You found $x = 3$ but dropped the negative sign in $y = -2(3)$. The product is $-6$.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A new labour contract at a regional warehouse sets a starting hourly wage of $\$20.00$ for all loaders. Under the contract, the hourly wage increases by $4\%$ every $2$ years.
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $w(t)$ is the hourly wage, in dollars, $t$ years after the contract begins?
items.explanation: The starting wage is 20 and each raise multiplies the wage by $1 + 0.04 = 1.04$. A raise happens once every 2 years, so after $t$ years there have been $\frac{t}{2}$ raises. That gives $w(t) = 20(1.04)^{t/2}$. As a check, $w(2) = 20(1.04) = 20.80$.

A.why: You multiplied $t$ by the 2-year interval when you should have divided by it. With this model the wage would go up four times in 2 years instead of once.

C.why: You used the percent, 0.04, as the growth factor. Each raise multiplies the wage by $1.04$. Multiplying by 0.04 would cut the wage to almost nothing.

D.why: You added a fixed $\$0.80$ for each 2-year period, which makes the model linear. A raise of a constant percentage compounds, so the model has to be exponential.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus:
A city's planning office tracks the number of registered users of its bike-share program. The table shows the number of users $t$ years after 2020. The number of users increased by the same percentage each year.

| $t$ | Registered users |
|---|---|
| 2 | 1,800 |
| 3 | 2,160 |
| 4 | 2,592 |
items.stem: Which of the following functions models this relationship, where $u(t)$ is the number of registered users $t$ years after 2020?
items.explanation: Each value is 1.2 times the one before it, since $2{,}160 \div 1{,}800 = 1.2$ and $2{,}592 \div 2{,}160 = 1.2$. The table starts at $t = 2$, so work back two years to get the value at $t = 0$: $1{,}800 \div 1.2^2 = 1{,}800 \div 1.44 = 1{,}250$. So $u(t) = 1{,}250(1.2)^t$. As a check, $u(3) = 1{,}250(1.728) = 2{,}160$.

B.why: You used the first row of the table as the starting amount. That row is $t = 2$, not $t = 0$, so this model gives 1,800 users in 2020.

C.why: You worked back only one year, from $t = 2$ to $t = 1$. You need one more step to reach $t = 0$.

D.why: You drew a straight line through the first two rows. It predicts 2,520 users at $t = 4$ instead of 2,592, because the users grow by a constant percentage, not a constant number.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: Archaeologists studying a sealed storage jar estimate that its residue first contained $96$ micrograms of an organic marker compound. The amount of the compound halves every $1{,}400$ years.
items.stem: How many years after the sample is sealed will exactly $6$ micrograms of the compound remain?
items.explanation: The model is $A(t) = 96(0.5)^{t/1{,}400}$. Halving from 96 goes 48, 24, 12, 6, so it takes 4 half-lives to reach 6 micrograms. Four half-lives is $4 \times 1{,}400 = 5{,}600$ years.

A.why: 4 is the number of half-lives, which is the value of $\frac{t}{1{,}400}$. You forgot to multiply by 1,400 to turn it into years.

B.why: You assumed the sample loses a fixed 48 micrograms every 1,400 years, which is a linear model. Halving removes less each time as the amount shrinks.

D.why: You took the ratio $96 \div 6 = 16$ as the number of half-lives. It actually means the amount was halved until it was $\frac{1}{16}$ of the start, and since $2^4 = 16$, that is 4 half-lives.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: In the tuning system used for a study of piano repertoire, the reference pitch has a frequency of $220$ hertz. Each time a note is $12$ semitones higher, its frequency doubles.
items.stem: What is the frequency, in hertz, of a note that is $36$ semitones above the reference pitch?
items.explanation: The model is $f(n) = 220(2)^{n/12}$, where $n$ is the number of semitones above the reference pitch. For $n = 36$ the exponent is $\frac{36}{12} = 3$, so $f(36) = 220(2)^3 = 220 \times 8 = 1{,}760$ hertz.

A.why: You multiplied 220 by 3, the number of doublings. Three doublings multiply by $2^3 = 8$, not by 3.

B.why: You added 220 hertz for every 12 semitones, as if the change were linear. Doubling is a constant factor, so each step adds more hertz than the one before.

D.why: You doubled four times instead of three. 36 semitones is $\frac{36}{12} = 3$ doublings.

items.subtype_name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
items.stimulus: A textile historian recreates a nineteenth-century madder dyeing process. As wool soaks in the dye bath, the concentration of dye left in the bath decreases by $20\%$ each hour. After $3$ hours, the concentration is $256$ milligrams per liter.
items.stem: Which of the following is closest to the concentration of dye, in milligrams per liter, in the bath at the start of the process?
items.explanation: Each hour the concentration is multiplied by $1 - 0.20 = 0.8$, so $C_0(0.8)^3 = 256$. Since $0.8^3 = 0.512$, you get $C_0 = 256 \div 0.512 = 500$ milligrams per liter.

A.why: You tried to undo each 20% decrease by multiplying by 1.2. A 20% increase does not reverse a 20% decrease. To go back one hour, divide by 0.8.

C.why: You added the three 20% losses to get 60% and divided 256 by 0.4. That treats the decrease as linear. Each 20% is taken from a smaller amount than the last.

D.why: You used 0.2 as the hourly factor, so you divided 256 by $0.2^3 = 0.008$. The bath keeps 80% each hour, so the factor is 0.8.

items.stimulus: Drypoint plates in printmaking wear down as prints are pulled from them. A printmaking studio gives a new plate a quality score of 100. Its model says that each print reduces the score by 10% of the score just before that print.
items.stem: According to the model, after which print does the plate's quality score first fall below 50?
items.explanation: After $n$ prints, the score is $100(0.9)^{n}$. After the 6th print it is $100(0.9)^{6} \approx 53.1$, which is still above 50. After the 7th print it is $100(0.9)^{7} \approx 47.8$. So the 7th print is the first one that brings the score below 50.

B.why: You subtracted 10 points per print, which is a linear model, and solved $100 - 10n = 50$. Each 10% is taken from a smaller score, so the losses shrink and the score falls more slowly.

C.why: After the 6th print the score is about 53.1, which is not yet below 50. That is the last print that keeps the score above 50, not the first one that drops it below.

items.subtype_name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
items.stimulus: Early pianos were built on wooden frames, which could not hold strings under high tension without warping. In the 1820s and 1830s, makers began adding cast-iron frames that could withstand much greater string tension. This let the strings be struck harder without going out of tune or breaking. ______ composers of the period began writing louder, more forceful passages than earlier keyboard music had allowed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The earlier sentences describe how iron frames let strings be struck harder. The last sentence gives the outcome: composers wrote louder music. You can put 'so' between them, which makes this a cause-and-effect relationship, and 'As a result' signals it.

A.why: You picked a time word, but 'previously' places the louder writing before the iron frames. The passage says the frames made that writing possible, so it must have come after.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. The composers' louder writing is not a sample of stronger frames. It is what the stronger frames led to, so the relationship is cause and effect, not example.

D.why: You read a contrast where there is none. Louder music follows naturally from strings that can be struck harder. It does not go against that point.

items.subtype_name: Lists: commas vs. semicolons for series items
items.stimulus: When a pathogen breaches the skin, the innate immune system dispatches several kinds of first responders. These include neutrophils, which engulf bacteria within minutes of an infection; macrophages, which digest cellular debris and release chemical signals that summon reinforcements______ natural killer cells, which destroy host cells already infected by a virus; and dendritic cells, which carry fragments of the invader to nearby lymph nodes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: This sentence lists four cell types, and each one carries its own 'which' clause set off by a comma. Because the items already contain commas, the list has to be separated by semicolons, and the writer does that everywhere else ('infection;' and 'virus;'). A semicolon after 'reinforcements' keeps the separators consistent and marks where the macrophage item ends and the natural killer item begins.

A.why: You looked only at the words around the blank, where a comma seems natural, and didn't check how the rest of the list is punctuated. The items contain internal commas and the other items are separated by semicolons, so a comma here blurs where one item stops and the next starts.

B.why: A colon introduces a list, an explanation, or an example. Natural killer cells don't explain macrophages; they are just the next item, so a colon in the middle of the series makes no sense.

D.why: A single dash works like a colon and marks an explanation or a sudden break. Nothing here is an explanation, and a dash doesn't match the semicolons that separate the other items.

items.subtype_name: Lists: commas vs. semicolons for series items
items.stimulus: The 2021 redesign of Corliss Avenue, long one of the city's most dangerous corridors, introduced protected bike lanes, separated from traffic by concrete planters; wider sidewalks, which now accommodate café seating in warmer months______ raised crosswalks at four intersections near the elementary school; and a bus-only lane during morning and evening rush hours.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: This sentence has a lot of commas, including the interrupter 'long one of the city's most dangerous corridors,' so you need the semicolons to see where each item stops. The first item ends at 'planters;' and the third at 'school;'. The blank separates the second item (wider sidewalks) from the third (raised crosswalks), so it must be a semicolon too.

A.why: A colon would present the raised crosswalks as an explanation of the wider sidewalks. They are a separate change in the same list, so a colon makes no sense between these items.

B.why: The comma before 'which now accommodate…' and the comma-heavy opening make one more comma look harmless. That's the trap. The items are separated by semicolons, and a comma here would run the sidewalks and crosswalks together.

C.why: A period ends the sentence partway through the list and leaves 'raised crosswalks…; and a bus-only lane…' as a fragment with no subject or verb.

items.subtype_name: Converting rates and squared/cubed units
items.stimulus: A folklore society is building a platform for a festival where performers retell regional legends. The platform will have a floor area of 48 square yards. The floor covering is sold for $2.50 per square foot.
items.stem: What is the total cost, in dollars, of the floor covering for the stage? (1 yard = 3 feet)
items.explanation: 1 yard = 3 feet, so 1 square yard = $3^2 = 9$ square feet. The platform covers $48 \times 9 = 432$ square feet. The cost is $432 \times 2.50 = 1{,}080$ dollars.

A.why: You multiplied by the linear factor 3 only once and got 144 square feet instead of squaring it. This is the classic squared-units trap: a square yard is 9 square feet, not 3.

B.why: 432 is the area in square feet, which is only partway to the answer. You stopped before multiplying by the price of $2.50 per square foot.

D.why: You cubed the factor and used 27 instead of squaring it to get 9. Cubing is for volume. This is an area, so the factor is applied twice.

items.subtype_name: Converting rates and squared/cubed units
items.stimulus: A seismologist studying a shallow earthquake records a compressional wave traveling through the crust at a constant speed of 5.4 kilometers per second.
items.stem: What is the speed of the wave, in kilometers per hour?
items.explanation: Only the time part of the unit changes, so the kilometers stay as they are. $5.4 \text{ km/s} \times \frac{3{,}600 \text{ s}}{1 \text{ h}} = 19{,}440$ km/h. The seconds cancel and you are left with kilometers per hour.

A.why: You divided by 3,600 when you should have multiplied, so the conversion factor was flipped. Write the units down: the seconds then fail to cancel.

B.why: Multiplying by 60 gives kilometers per minute, which is halfway there. You still need to multiply by 60 again to get from minutes to hours.

D.why: You converted both parts of the rate and also changed kilometers to meters. The question keeps kilometers, so only the time part should change.

items.stimulus: During a breeding-season survey of a salt-marsh tern colony, an ornithologist found an average density of 0.04 nests per square foot.
items.stem: Which of the following is closest to the average number of nests per square yard in the colony? (1 yard = 3 feet)
items.explanation: A square yard is $3^2 = 9$ square feet, so it holds 9 times as many nests as a square foot: $0.04 \times 9 = 0.36$ nests per square yard. items.stimulus: On a survey map of a coastal region, 1 centimeter represents an actual distance of 2.5 kilometers. A protected wetland in the region has an actual area of 50 square kilometers.
items.stem: What is the area, in square centimeters, of the wetland on the map?
items.explanation: 1 square centimeter on the map represents $2.5^2 = 6.25$ square kilometers. The wetland's area on the map is $50 \div 6.25 = 8$ square centimeters.

D.why: You squared the factor correctly but multiplied instead of dividing. That converts in the wrong direction, from map units to real units.

items.subtype_name: Between / min-max range → double inequality
items.stimulus: A seismologist sorts recorded earthquakes into bands by magnitude. An earthquake goes in the moderate band if its magnitude is at least 5.0 but less than 6.0.
items.stem: Which inequality represents this situation, where $m$ is the magnitude of an earthquake placed in the moderate band?
items.explanation: "At least 5.0" means 5.0 is allowed, so you use $5.0 \le m$. "Less than 6.0" is strict, so you use $m < 6.0$. Putting them together with the lower bound on the left gives $5.0 \le m < 6.0$.

A.why: You paired the phrases with the wrong numbers. You made 5.0 strict and 6.0 inclusive, but the text says "at least" 5.0 and "less than" 6.0.

C.why: You used $\le$ at both ends. "Less than 6.0" is strict, so a magnitude of exactly 6.0 is not in the moderate band.

D.why: You put the bounds the wrong way round. 6.0 is the upper limit, not the lower one, and no number can be at least 6.0 and also less than 5.0.

items.stimulus: A printmaker is pulling 20 prints from a carved linoleum block. Each print uses at least 4 milliliters and at most 6 milliliters of ink.
items.stem: Which inequality represents this situation, where $k$ is the total amount of ink, in milliliters, used for the 20 prints?
items.explanation: The range is per print, so you multiply both ends by 20: $4 \times 20 = 80$ and $6 \times 20 = 120$. "At least" and "at most" both include the endpoint, so $80 \le k \le 120$.

A.why: This is the range for one print. $k$ is the total for all 20 prints, so you need to scale both ends by 20.

B.why: You added 20 to each end instead of multiplying by 20. Twenty prints at 4 to 6 milliliters each means 20 times as much ink.

D.why: You used strict signs. "At least" and "at most" include the endpoints, so totals of exactly 80 and 120 milliliters are possible.

items.explanation: The total water, $w + 10$, must satisfy $25 \le w + 10 \le 40$. Subtracting 10 from every part gives $15 \le w \le 30$. A minimum and a maximum both include their endpoints.

C.why: You subtracted the 10 millimeters of rain from the lower bound only. You have to subtract it from both ends of the range.

D.why: You used strict signs. A minimum and a maximum include their endpoints, so adding exactly 15 or exactly 30 millimeters is allowed.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse spends its days picking parasites off larger reef fish. A sentence that overturns an expectation needs a contrast word, and 'However' is the only contrast word among the choices.

B.why: 'Similarly' says the second sentence matches the first. The study contradicts the assumption instead of repeating it.

D.why: 'For instance' would make the study one example of the belief that clients come only for parasite removal. The study is evidence against that belief, not an example of it.

items.stimulus: Standard labor-market models predict that a sharp minimum-wage increase will shrink teenage employment, since teenagers are usually the least experienced workers on a payroll. items.stimulus: A city planner is designing two triangular pocket parks. Park $PQR$ has a right angle at $Q$, and the measure of angle $R$ is $34^\circ$. C.why: You subtracted only the $34^\circ$ angle from $180^\circ$ and forgot about the right angle at $Q$. $146^\circ$ is the supplement of angle $R$, not a remaining angle of the triangle.

D.why: You found angle $P = 56^\circ$ correctly and then multiplied it by the scale factor 3. Dilating a figure scales its sides, but corresponding angles stay equal.

When seismic waves pass from hard bedrock into soft sediment, they slow down. Their amplitude grows as they slow, so the ground shakes harder. After a moderate earthquake in 2024, seismologist Ines Kovač compared readings from five monitoring stations. She concluded that, among stations the same distance from the epicenter, those built on sediment recorded stronger shaking than those built on bedrock. For example, ______

Peak Ground Acceleration at Five Stations, 2024 Earthquake
Station | Distance from epicenter (km) | Ground type | Peak acceleration (% g)
S1 | 12 | Bedrock | 9
S2 | 12 | Sediment | 21
S3 | 30 | Bedrock | 4
S4 | 30 | Sediment | 11
S5 | 8 | Sediment | 26
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: Station S5, on sediment 8 km from the epicenter, recorded 26% g, whereas Station S3, on bedrock 30 km away, recorded 4% g.
Station S3, on bedrock 30 km from the epicenter, recorded 4% g, whereas Station S4, on sediment 30 km away, recorded 11% g.
Station S2, on sediment 12 km from the epicenter, recorded 21% g, whereas Station S4, on sediment 30 km away, recorded 11% g.
Station S1, on bedrock 12 km from the epicenter, recorded 21% g, whereas Station S2, on sediment 12 km away, recorded 9% g.
items.explanation: Kovač's claim is limited to stations the same distance from the epicenter. So you need two stations at one distance, one on each ground type, with the sediment station shaking harder. S3 and S4 are both 30 km away, and S4, on sediment, recorded 11% g against S3's 4% g on bedrock.

A.why: The numbers are right, and sediment does beat bedrock here, but you missed the scope words 'the same distance.' S5 is much closer to the epicenter than S3, so distance could explain the whole gap, and the choice can't show that ground type made the difference.

C.why: This is an accurate reading, but both stations sit on sediment. You are comparing distances when the claim is about ground type, so the choice shows that shaking weakens farther away, which is a different point.

D.why: You swapped the values. S1 on bedrock recorded 9% g and S2 on sediment recorded 21% g, so this choice reverses the direction the table shows.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
In the widely told tale of the stolen fire, the thief is a clever animal whose species varies from place to place. Folklorist Amara Oyelaran catalogued 412 recorded versions of the tale from four regions. She argues that the trickster's form reflects the storytellers' landscape more than their language: even where the same language is spoken, coastal and inland communities favor different tricksters. For instance, ______

Versions of the Stolen-Fire Tale by Region
Region | Language | Setting | Versions with a heron trickster (%)
Varnel | Oskan | Coastal | 72
Dorrow | Oskan | Inland | 18
Pelle | Mirran | Coastal | 69
Istek | Mirran | Inland | 21
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: 72% of versions from coastal Varnel feature a heron trickster, compared with 21% of versions from inland Istek.
72% of versions from coastal Varnel feature a heron trickster, compared with 69% of versions from coastal Pelle.
72% of versions from inland Dorrow feature a heron trickster, compared with 18% of versions from coastal Varnel.
72% of versions from coastal Varnel feature a heron trickster, compared with 18% of versions from inland Dorrow.
items.explanation: The example has to show two communities that share a language but differ in setting, with different tricksters. Varnel and Dorrow both speak Oskan. Coastal Varnel uses the heron in 72% of versions and inland Dorrow in only 18%, so landscape, not language, accounts for the difference.

A.why: The figures are correct and the setting differs, but you overlooked 'even where the same language is spoken.' Varnel speaks Oskan and Istek speaks Mirran, so language could explain the gap as well as landscape could.

B.why: This is accurate, but it shows two coastal regions being similar. The sentence has to show coastal and inland communities differing within a single language, and this pair differs in language, not setting.

C.why: You attached each figure to the wrong region. Dorrow is inland with 18% and Varnel is coastal with 72%, so this choice reverses the pattern.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
Soluble fiber such as oat beta-glucan forms a gel in the stomach. The gel slows how quickly food reaches the small intestine, and so how fast glucose enters the blood. A research team gave adults with either normal or impaired glucose tolerance a standard breakfast, or the same breakfast with added beta-glucan. The team concluded that the fiber's benefit was not uniform: it blunted the post-meal glucose rise considerably more in adults with impaired tolerance. For example, ______

Average Rise in Blood Glucose After Breakfast (mg/dL)
Group | Standard breakfast | Breakfast with beta-glucan
Normal tolerance | 48 | 41
Impaired tolerance | 92 | 63
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: the fiber reduced the glucose rise by 29 mg/dL in adults with impaired tolerance but by only 7 mg/dL in adults with normal tolerance.
the fiber reduced the glucose rise from 92 mg/dL to 63 mg/dL in adults with impaired tolerance, a drop of nearly one-third.
impaired-tolerance adults eating the fiber breakfast had a larger rise (63 mg/dL) than normal adults eating the standard one (48 mg/dL).
the fiber reduced the glucose rise by 7 mg/dL in adults with impaired tolerance but by 29 mg/dL in adults with normal tolerance.
items.explanation: The claim is comparative: the fiber helped one group more than the other. To show that, you need the size of the fiber's effect in both groups. It was 92 − 63 = 29 mg/dL for impaired tolerance and 48 − 41 = 7 mg/dL for normal tolerance, and only this choice puts those two numbers side by side.

B.why: This is accurate, and it does show the fiber working in impaired-tolerance adults. But the claim is that the benefit was larger in that group than in the other, and this choice never mentions the normal-tolerance group, so nothing is compared.

C.why: Both numbers are correct, but you compared people on different breakfasts from different groups. That shows impaired-tolerance adults still have higher spikes, not that the fiber did more for them.

D.why: You attached the reductions to the wrong groups. The 29 mg/dL drop belongs to the impaired-tolerance group, so this choice reverses the finding.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
Economists have argued that offering remote work reduces quitting mainly because it spares employees costly commutes. If that explanation is correct, the option should matter little at firms where commutes are already short. Analyzing records from 2,300 mid-sized firms, labor economist Tomás Reyes found that this prediction held: ______

Annual Quit Rates at Mid-Sized Firms
Average commute | Remote option offered | Quit rate (%)
Long | Yes | 11
Long | No | 19
Short | Yes | 12
Short | No | 13
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: firms with long commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 11%, compared with 19% for long-commute firms that did not.
firms with short commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 12%, compared with 19% for long-commute firms that did not.
firms with short commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 12%, compared with 13% for short-commute firms that did not.
firms with short commutes that offered remote work had a quit rate of 12%, compared with 19% for short-commute firms that did not.
items.explanation: The prediction is about short-commute firms only: there, remote work should make little difference. So you need the two short-commute groups, with and without the option. Their quit rates are 12% and 13%, which are nearly the same, and that is exactly what the prediction expects.

A.why: This is a true and striking comparison, but it concerns long-commute firms. The prediction Reyes tested was that the option matters little where commutes are short, and a big effect at long-commute firms doesn't show that.

B.why: The numbers are accurate, but the two firms differ in both commute length and remote policy. A mismatched pair can't isolate what remote work does at short-commute firms.

D.why: You misread the table. Short-commute firms without remote work had a 13% quit rate, not 19%, and the false figure would suggest a large effect, the opposite of what Reyes found.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
In most metals, shrinking the crystal grains raises hardness, because the boundaries between grains block the dislocations that let a metal deform. Materials scientist Hye-jin Park suspected that this effect has a limit. When grains become extremely small, she reasoned, the boundaries themselves begin to slide, and hardness should drop. Testing nickel samples of varying grain size, Park found evidence of such a reversal: ______

Hardness of Nickel Samples by Grain Size
Sample | Average grain size (nm) | Hardness (GPa)
P | 200 | 3.1
Q | 80 | 4.4
R | 35 | 5.6
S | 18 | 6.0
T | 8 | 5.2
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: the sample with 200 nm grains had a hardness of 3.1 GPa, while the sample with 35 nm grains had a hardness of 5.6 GPa.
the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa, while the sample with 200 nm grains had a hardness of 3.1 GPa.
the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 6.0 GPa, while the sample with 18 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa.
the sample with 18 nm grains had a hardness of 6.0 GPa, while the sample with 8 nm grains had a hardness of 5.2 GPa.
items.explanation: A reversal means that at the smallest sizes, smaller grains give lower hardness, the opposite of the usual trend. Going from 18 nm to 8 nm, hardness falls from 6.0 GPa to 5.2 GPa. That is the drop Park predicted.

A.why: This is accurate, but it shows the ordinary trend, where smaller grains mean harder metal. The sentence promises evidence of a reversal, and this pair shows the rule working as usual.

B.why: Both figures are correct, but comparing the smallest grains with the largest just shows that 8 nm nickel is harder than 200 nm nickel, which fits the usual trend. The reversal only appears when you compare the two smallest sizes.

C.why: You swapped the hardness values. The 18 nm sample measured 6.0 GPa and the 8 nm sample 5.2 GPa, so this version would make the smallest grains hardest, which is no reversal at all.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
Over the past fifty years, a new pronunciation of the vowel in words like "boat" has spread outward from the city of Aldren. Dialect geographers long assumed that such changes move like ripples, reaching nearer towns first. After surveying four towns, linguist Petra Lindqvist concluded that travel links can matter more than sheer distance: a town tied to Aldren by rail may be further along in the change than a town that sits closer but lacks a rail link. For example, ______

Use of the New Vowel in Four Towns
Town | Distance from Aldren (km) | Rail link | Speakers using new vowel (%)
Brisk | 40 | Yes | 57
Coll | 95 | No | 33
Eske | 150 | Yes | 49
Dunmere | 160 | No | 12
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: 49% of speakers in Eske, 150 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 33% in Coll, 95 km away without one.
49% of speakers in Eske, 150 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 12% in Dunmere, 160 km away without one.
57% of speakers in Brisk, 40 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 33% in Coll, 95 km away without one.
33% of speakers in Eske, 150 km away with a rail link, use the new vowel, compared with 49% in Coll, 95 km away without one.
items.explanation: The claim needs a rail town that is farther from Aldren and still further along in the change than a closer town without rail. Eske is 150 km away with rail and has 49%. Coll is only 95 km away without rail and has 33%. The ripple model can't explain that, but rail can.

B.why: This is accurate, and the rail town does lead. But Dunmere is farther from Aldren than Eske, so plain distance could explain Eske's lead. The claim specifically needs the town without rail to be the closer one.

C.why: The numbers are right, but Brisk is both closer to Aldren and on the rail line. Its lead fits the ripple model just as well, so it can't show that rail outweighs distance.

D.why: You swapped the two towns' percentages. Eske has 49% and Coll has 33%, and the reversed figures would make the rail town lag behind.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
Many reef fish spend their larval stage in open water, then locate a reef partly by listening for the crackle of snapping shrimp and the calls of resident fish. Marine biologist Kalani Akana tested whether ocean warming interferes with this behavior. She placed clownfish larvae in four tanks, each broadcasting sound recorded at either a healthy or a degraded reef, at one of two temperatures. Akana concluded that warmer water blunts larvae's response to healthy-reef sound. For example, ______

Clownfish Larvae Settlement by Tank
Tank | Recording | Water temperature (°C) | Larvae settled (%)
1 | Healthy reef | 26 | 58
2 | Degraded reef | 26 | 31
3 | Healthy reef | 30 | 34
4 | Degraded reef | 30 | 29
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: 58% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 26°C, compared with 31% of larvae hearing degraded-reef sound at 26°C.
34% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 30°C, compared with 29% of larvae hearing degraded-reef sound at 30°C.
58% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 26°C, compared with 34% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound at 30°C.
34% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound settled at 26°C, compared with 58% of larvae hearing healthy-reef sound at 30°C.
items.explanation: To show that warmth blunts the response to healthy-reef sound, keep the recording the same and change only the temperature. Tanks 1 and 3 both played healthy-reef sound. Settlement fell from 58% at 26°C to 34% at 30°C.

A.why: This is a correct reading, but both tanks were at 26°C. It shows that larvae prefer healthy-reef sound, which is the behavior being studied, not that warming weakens it.

B.why: The figures are accurate, but both tanks were at 30°C. Without a cooler comparison you can't tell from this pair whether warming changed anything.

D.why: You swapped the temperatures. 58% settled at 26°C and 34% at 30°C, and the reversed version would suggest warming strengthens the response.

items.subtype_name: Use the data to complete the example
items.stimulus:
Plants absorb carbon dioxide through tiny leaf pores called stomata. When atmospheric CO₂ is abundant, a plant can take in enough through fewer pores, so leaves grown in CO₂-rich air tend to have lower stomatal density. After examining fossil ginkgo leaves from rock layers spanning an ancient warming event, paleobotanist Rafael Quintero concluded that CO₂ rose during the event and then returned to earlier levels. For example, ______

Stomatal Density of Fossil Ginkgo Leaves
Layer | Age (million years ago) | Timing | Stomata per mm²
1 | 56.4 | Before event | 142
2 | 56.0 | During event | 88
3 | 55.8 | During event | 91
4 | 55.2 | After event | 137
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: stomatal density fell from 142 per mm² before the event to 88 per mm² during it, a decline of nearly 40%.
stomatal density fell from 142 per mm² before the event to 88 during it and then rose to 137 afterward.
stomatal density was 88 per mm² in the earlier layer from the event and 91 in the later layer from it.
stomatal density rose from 88 per mm² before the event to 142 during it and then fell to 137 afterward.
items.explanation: Quintero's conclusion has two parts: CO₂ rose, then came back down. Because density moves opposite to CO₂, you need a drop during the event and a recovery after it. This choice shows both: 142 fell to 88 and then rose to 137.

A.why: This is accurate and supports the first half of the conclusion, that CO₂ rose. But it stops before the event ends, so it says nothing about CO₂ returning to earlier levels.

C.why: Both values are correct, but both come from during the event. Two nearly equal readings from inside the event can't show a rise or a return.

D.why: You misplaced the values. Density was 142 before the event and 88 during it, and the reversed order would suggest CO₂ fell during the warming.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Winter cover crops such as cereal rye are planted after harvest and killed in spring, which leaves a layer of residue on the soil surface. That residue slows evaporation, so the soil under it holds more water into midsummer, when corn is most sensitive to moisture stress. Agronomists at a Nebraska research farm compared corn grown after rye with corn grown on bare soil over eight seasons, four wet and four dry. They concluded that a rye cover crop raises corn yields in dry seasons, when the extra stored water matters most.

Average Corn Yield (bushels per acre)
Season type | Bare soil | After rye
Wet | 182 | 176
Dry | 131 | 154
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the agronomists' conclusion?
choices: In wet seasons, corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre, while corn grown after rye yielded 176.
Corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre in wet seasons but only 131 bushels per acre in dry seasons.
In dry seasons, corn grown after rye yielded 154 bushels per acre, while corn grown on bare soil yielded 131.
Corn grown after rye yielded more per acre than corn grown on bare soil in both wet seasons and dry seasons.
items.explanation: The conclusion is limited to dry seasons and compares rye with bare soil. So you need the dry row, with rye higher than bare soil. Choice C gives exactly that: 154 bushels against 131.

A.why: You ignored the condition the claim depends on. The conclusion is about dry seasons, and this choice reports only the wet row. In that row rye doesn't even raise yields.

B.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice holds the treatment fixed at bare soil and compares weather conditions. That shows drought lowers yield, not that rye raises it.

D.why: You misread the wet row. In wet seasons corn after rye yielded 176 bushels, less than the 182 bushels on bare soil.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
When seismic waves pass from hard bedrock into the soft sediments that fill many valleys, they slow down and grow in amplitude, so the ground shakes harder. Seismologists express this as an amplification factor: peak shaking at a sediment site divided by peak shaking at a nearby bedrock site. Distant earthquakes arrive dominated by long-period waves, which sediment layers tend to resonate with. For that reason, one team hypothesized that basin sediments amplify shaking from distant earthquakes more than shaking from nearby ones.

Average Peak Ground Acceleration (cm/s²)
Earthquake distance | Bedrock sites | Sediment sites
Under 50 km | 120 | 180
Over 150 km | 20 | 50
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the team's hypothesis?
choices: For nearby earthquakes, sediment sites exceeded bedrock sites by 60 cm/s², whereas for distant ones the gap was only 30 cm/s².
Sediment sites recorded stronger shaking than bedrock sites did for both nearby earthquakes and distant earthquakes.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for nearby earthquakes but 1.5 times for distant ones.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for distant earthquakes but 1.5 times for nearby ones.
items.explanation: The passage defines amplification as a ratio, sediment divided by bedrock. So you have to compute it: 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 for distant earthquakes and 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5 for nearby ones. Choice D shows that distant earthquakes are amplified more, which is what the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You used raw differences when the passage defined amplification as a ratio. The gaps are accurate, but subtraction doesn't measure the amplification factor. Measured as a ratio, the result goes the other way.

B.why: You chose a true statement that supports a broader claim, that sediments amplify shaking at all. The hypothesis is about which distance is amplified more, and this choice doesn't compare the two.

C.why: You reversed the ratios. Nearby earthquakes give 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5, and distant ones give 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, not the other way around.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Hillshading simulates the shadows that terrain casts under light from one direction. It is often added to contour maps to make relief easier to see. Cartographer Tomasz Wierzbicki asked novice and experienced map readers to identify the easiest walking routes on contour-only or hillshaded versions of the same maps. Experienced readers can already picture terrain from contour lines alone. Wierzbicki therefore hypothesized that hillshading would improve novices' accuracy more than it would improve experienced readers' accuracy.

Route Choices Judged Correct (%)
Reader group | Contour-only map | Hillshaded map
Novice | 58 | 64
Experienced | 71 | 83
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken Wierzbicki's hypothesis?
choices: Hillshading raised experienced readers' accuracy by 12 percentage points but raised novices' accuracy by only 6 points.
Novices chose correct routes 64% of the time with hillshaded maps and 58% of the time with contour-only maps.
Experienced readers chose correct routes more often than novices did with both contour-only and hillshaded maps.
Hillshading raised novices' accuracy by 12 percentage points but raised experienced readers' accuracy by only 6 points.
items.explanation: The hypothesis predicts that the novices' gain from hillshading will be larger than the experienced readers' gain. To weaken it, you need the opposite. Experienced readers gained 12 points (71 to 83), and novices gained only 6 (58 to 64). Choice A states that.

B.why: You stopped at one group. This choice shows that novices improved, but the hypothesis compares the size of the improvement across both groups. A single row can't weaken that comparison.

Economists who study employee turnover often find that workers leave jobs when their schedules clash with obligations outside work. Remote eligibility cut caregivers' quit rate from 18% to 9% but changed non-caregivers' rate only from 11% to 10%.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
Vaccine adjuvants are added to stimulate the innate immune cells that help launch an antibody response, and these cells become less responsive with age. Researchers gave younger and older adults a flu vaccine with or without an experimental adjuvant. They measured antibody titers before vaccination and four weeks after. Because baseline titers differ by age, they compared groups using the fold rise: the post-vaccination titer divided by the pre-vaccination titer. They hypothesized that the adjuvant would benefit older adults more than younger adults.

Mean Antibody Titer
Group | Pre-vaccination | Post-vaccination
Younger, standard vaccine | 50 | 400
Younger, with adjuvant | 50 | 500
Older, standard vaccine | 10 | 30
Older, with adjuvant | 10 | 90
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: The adjuvant raised younger adults' post-vaccination titer by 100, compared with a rise of only 60 for older adults.
The adjuvant raised older adults' fold rise from 3 to 9 but raised younger adults' fold rise only from 8 to 10.
Older adults given the adjuvant reached a titer of 90, three times the 30 reached with the standard vaccine.
Older adults given the adjuvant showed a larger fold rise than younger adults given the same adjuvant did.
items.explanation: The researchers measure benefit using fold rise, so you have to compute it for all four rows. For older adults, fold rise went from 3 (30 ÷ 10) to 9 (90 ÷ 10). For younger adults, it went from 8 (400 ÷ 50) to 10 (500 ÷ 50). Older adults gained far more, as the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You used raw titers when the passage said groups are compared by fold rise. The differences of 100 and 60 are accurate. But because baselines differ so much, raw gains don't measure the benefit the researchers defined.

D.why: You misread the adjuvant rows. With the adjuvant, older adults' fold rise was 9 and younger adults' was 10, so older adults' fold rise was not larger. The hypothesis concerns the size of the gain, not the final fold rise.

items.subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
items.stimulus:
In a highly reverberant building, each note an organ plays lingers for several seconds, and rapid passages can blur into an indistinct wash. Musicologist Inês Carvalho compared recordings of the same organists performing in acoustically dry churches and in reverberant cathedrals. She reasoned that because blurring is worst when notes follow one another quickly, players would compensate by slowing down. She claimed that reverberation reduces tempo more in fast pieces than in slow ones.

Average Tempo (beats per minute)
Piece type | Dry church | Reverberant cathedral
Fast | 132 | 112
Slow | 64 | 60
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Carvalho's claim?
choices: Organists slowed fast pieces by 20 beats per minute in reverberant cathedrals but slowed slow pieces by only 4.
Organists played both fast and slow pieces at lower tempos in reverberant cathedrals than in dry churches.
In reverberant cathedrals, organists played fast pieces at 112 beats per minute and slow pieces at 60.
Organists slowed slow pieces by 20 beats per minute in reverberant cathedrals but slowed fast pieces by only 4.
items.explanation: Carvalho's claim compares the size of the slowdown in the two kinds of piece. Fast pieces dropped from 132 to 112, a fall of 20 beats per minute. Slow pieces dropped from 64 to 60, a fall of 4. Choice A makes that comparison.

B.why: You chose an accurate statement that supports a weaker claim, that reverberation slows tempo in general. Carvalho claims the effect is larger for fast pieces, and this choice doesn't compare the size of the two slowdowns.

C.why: You compared the wrong cells. This choice compares fast and slow pieces within the cathedral column. Fast pieces are faster everywhere, so this says nothing about the effect of reverberation.
