items.stimulus:
A paleobotanist compares two linear rules relating $x$, the leaf width of a fossil, and $y$, its vein density. The rules form the system below.

$6x + ky = 9$
$2x + 4y = 3$
items.stem: In the given system of equations, $k$ is a constant. For which values of $k$ does the system have at least one solution?
items.explanation: Multiplying the second equation by $3$ gives $6x + 12y = 9$. So when $k = 12$, the two equations are the same line and there are infinitely many solutions. For any other value of $k$, the $x$-coefficients still have ratio $3$ but the $y$-coefficients don't, so the slopes differ and the lines cross exactly once. Either way the system has at least one solution, so every real value of $k$ works.

C.why: You answered the opposite question, which values of $k$ give no solution. No value does, but this question asks when there is at least one solution, and that is true for every $k$.

items.subtype_name: Infinitely many solutions (the same line)
items.stimulus:
A musicologist relates $x$, the number of bars in a passage, and $y$, its tempo marking, using two equations taken from separate catalogues of the same composer's work.

$3x - y = 4$
$px + qy = r$
items.stem:
In the given system of equations, $p$, $q$, and $r$ are constants. If the system has infinitely many solutions, which of the following must be true?

I. $q = -\frac{p}{3}$
II. $r = 4$
items.explanation: Infinitely many solutions means the second equation is the first multiplied by some nonzero number $t$. So $p = 3t$, $q = -t$, and $r = 4t$. Statement I always holds, because $-\frac{p}{3} = -t = q$. Statement II holds only when $t = 1$. For example, $6x - 2y = 8$ is the same line with $r = 8$. Only statement I must be true.

B.why: You made a sign error with the slope. The line $3x - y = 4$ has slope $3$, and matching that requires $q = -\frac{p}{3}$, not $q = \frac{p}{3}$. Statement I is true, and statement II is not required.

C.why: You assumed the second equation must have the same constant as the first. The constants only need to be in the same ratio as the coefficients, so $r = 4t$ for any nonzero $t$, not necessarily $4$.

D.why: You treated infinitely many solutions as two lines crossing, so you expected different slopes and rejected I. Identical lines must have the same slope, which is exactly what statement I says.

items.stimulus: An astronomy student selected 60 asteroids at random from a catalog of 1,500 main-belt asteroids and looked up the diameter of each one. items.stem: Based on these results, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: It is plausible that the mean diameter of all 1,500 asteroids in the catalog is between 11 and 17 kilometers.
It is plausible that every asteroid in the catalog has a diameter between 11 and 17 kilometers.

items.stimulus: An ecologist reintroduced a population of red-spotted newts to a restored wetland. The function $P(t) = 240(1.15)^{t/2}$ gives the estimated number of newts in the wetland $t$ years after the reintroduction.
items.stem: Which of the following is the best interpretation of $1.15$ in this context?
choices: The estimated newt population increases by 15% every year.
The estimated newt population increases by 1.15 newts every 2 years.
The estimated newt population increases by 15% every 2 years.
The estimated newt population increases by 115% every 2 years.
items.explanation: The base $1.15$ is what the population is multiplied by each time the exponent goes up by 1. Multiplying by $1.15$ is the same as a 15% increase. The exponent is $t/2$, so it goes up by 1 only when $t$ goes up by 2. That means the population grows by 15% every 2 years.

A.why: You read the 15% growth correctly but missed the exponent $t/2$. It grows by 1 only every 2 years, so the 15% increase happens every 2 years, not every year.

B.why: You treated the base of the exponential as an amount added each time. In fact $1.15$ is a multiplier, which means a percentage increase, not 1.15 more newts.

D.why: You turned the multiplier $1.15$ into 115% growth. Multiplying by $1.15$ keeps 100% of the population and adds 15%, so the increase is 15%, not 115%.

The number of prints the studio produces for each dollar
The total cost, in dollars, of producing a single print
items.explanation: $3$ is the coefficient on $p$, so it is the rate: each extra print adds $3$ dollars to the total cost. The units are dollars per print, which are the units of $C$ divided by the units of $p$.

The number of years it takes to add one docking station
The number of docking stations added to the network each year

items.subtype_name: Run-on / comma splice: join or split two full sentences
items.stimulus: After an infection clears, most of the antibody-producing cells that fought it die off, but a small population of memory B cells remains. These cells can persist in the body for decades after the pathogen is gone ______ circulating at low levels, they respond within days if the same pathogen reappears, producing antibodies far faster than they did during the first encounter.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The words before the blank form a complete sentence: 'These cells can persist in the body for decades after the pathogen is gone.' The words after it also form a complete sentence. Its subject and verb are 'they respond', and 'circulating at low levels' is only an introductory phrase. Two complete sentences can be joined with a semicolon, so you should choose this option.

A.why: You took 'circulating at low levels' as a modifier attached to the first sentence. But 'they respond' gives the second half its own subject and verb, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.

C.why: With no punctuation, two complete sentences run together into a fused run-on. The reader can't tell where the first thought ends.

D.why: You added 'and' without a comma before it. That runs the two sentences together, and 'and circulating at low levels, they respond' still leaves a comma splice after 'levels.'

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: Historians have often cited dye analyses of surviving seventeenth-century Dutch woolens as evidence that blue was the period's most popular color for everyday clothing: nearly 60 percent of the tested fragments contain indigo or woad. However, those blue dyes bind to wool far more stably than the era's weld-based yellows and madder-based reds, which fade and wash out over decades of wear. The high share of blue among the fragments therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: shows that red and yellow woolens were in fact more common than blue ones during the period.
may reflect which dyes endured over time rather than which colors people most often chose to wear.
indicates that seventeenth-century dyers favored indigo because it held up better than other dyes.
suggests that dye analysis cannot identify the plant sources used in faded wool fragments.
items.explanation: The problem is a survival bias. Blue dyes last, and reds and yellows fade away, so the fragments that still show color are skewed toward blue. That makes the link between 'what survives' and 'what people wore' uncertain. It doesn't show that any other color was more popular. Choice B states only that uncertainty.

A.why: You treated the complication as proof of the opposite. Fading dyes make the blue share unreliable, but nothing shows red or yellow was actually more common.

C.why: You added a step that isn't in the passage. The text says blue dyes last longer on surviving cloth. It says nothing about why dyers chose them or whether they knew this.

D.why: You focused on the lab method instead of what the 60 percent figure can show. The passage never says analysis fails on faded fragments. Its point is about which colors survived.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: In a survey of 3,000 adults, those who reported eating the most added sugar had, on average, lower body mass indexes than those who reported eating the least. Intake was measured with a single 24-hour dietary recall, however, and validation studies have found that adults with higher body mass indexes tend to underreport sugary foods more than other adults do. The survey's finding therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: indicates that a single 24-hour recall is the most common way researchers measure diet.
shows that higher-BMI adults underreport sugar because they are trying to lose weight.
may stem partly from differences in reporting accuracy rather than in what people actually ate.
demonstrates that lower-BMI adults actually consume more added sugar than other adults do.
items.explanation: The problem is that one group underreports more than the others. If higher-BMI adults leave out more sugary foods, their reported intake looks lower than it really is, and that alone could produce the pattern. So the finding might not reflect real differences in diet. Choice C says exactly that and claims nothing firmer.

A.why: You grabbed a detail about the method. The passage never says how common the recall method is, and that doesn't explain what the flaw means for the finding.

B.why: You supplied a cause the passage never gives. The text says higher-BMI adults underreport more. It doesn't say why.

D.why: You trusted the reported numbers even though the passage just gave you a reason to doubt them. Biased reporting makes the pattern uncertain, so it can't confirm a firm claim about actual intake.

items.stimulus: Engineers testing a new concrete mix subjected sample slabs to 300 freeze-thaw cycles, after which the slabs showed less surface scaling than slabs of conventional concrete did. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: may not accurately predict how the new mix will perform on highways that are routinely salted.
show that the new mix will scale faster than conventional concrete once it is exposed to salt.
indicate that de-icing salts damage the new mix more severely than plain freezing water does.
show that the new mix scaled more than conventional concrete did under freeze-thaw cycling.
items.explanation: The flaw is that the test left out salt, which real roads face and which speeds up scaling in some mixes. C.why: You missed the word 'some.' Salt speeds up scaling in some mixes, and the passage never says the new mix is one of them.

D.why: You reversed the reported result. The passage says the new mix scaled less than conventional concrete.

items.stimulus: After a school district launched a handwashing campaign, officials credited it with a 20 percent drop in illness-related absences compared with the previous winter. items.stimulus: Comparing a 1712 nautical chart of a stretch of the Normandy coast with modern satellite imagery, a geographer found that the charted shoreline lies about 400 meters seaward of today's. choices: proves that the coast has eroded far less since 1712 than the comparison implies.

items.subtype_name: The conclusion has to hedge
items.stimulus: Some seismologists have proposed that an earthquake that struck the region in 1787 was among the largest in its recorded history, citing colonial accounts describing widespread building collapses across dozens of settlements. items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus: A printmaking studio has two etching presses. Working alone, the older press finishes a run of posters in $a$ hours and the newer press finishes the same run in $b$ hours. Working together, they finish the run in $T$ hours, where $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$.
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $T$, $a$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $a$ in terms of $T$ and $b$?
items.explanation: First isolate the reciprocal: $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. Over the common denominator $Tb$ this is $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{b - T}{Tb}$. Then take reciprocals of both sides to get $a = \frac{Tb}{b - T}$. As a check, with $T = 2$ and $b = 3$ the original equation gives $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{6}$, so $a = 6$, and $\frac{2 \cdot 3}{3 - 2} = 6$.

A.why: You flipped each fraction separately, turning $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ into $T = a + b$. You can't undo a sum of reciprocals one term at a time.

B.why: This is $\frac{1}{a}$, not $a$. You combined the fractions correctly but skipped the last step of taking the reciprocal.

D.why: You reversed the subtraction when combining $\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. The numerator should be $b - T$. Your version gives a negative time, because two presses together finish faster than either press alone, so $T < b$.

items.stimulus: A meteorologist estimates the total pressure $P$ on a weather-station sensor using $P = \frac{d v^2}{2} + s$. Here $d$ is the air density, $v$ is the wind speed, and $s$ is the static air pressure.

items.stimulus: A linguist compares a bilingual corpus in which $w$ sentences are in Welsh and $n$ sentences are in English, where $w > n$. The linguist measures the corpus's imbalance with the index $R = \frac{w - n}{w + n}$.

items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $w + n$ to get $Rw + Rn = w - n$. Collect the $w$ terms on one side: $Rn + n = w - Rw$. Factor both sides: $n(1 + R) = w(1 - R)$. C.why: You dropped a sign when you moved $Rw$ across. Since $R < 1$, the denominator $R - 1$ is negative, so this choice makes $w$ negative, which breaks the condition that $w$ is positive.

items.explanation: Isolate the reciprocal: $\frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b} = \frac{b - T}{bT}$. Take reciprocals of both sides: $a = \frac{bT}{b - T}$. Check: with $a = 6$ and $b = 3$, $T = 2$, and $\frac{3 \cdot 2}{3 - 2} = 6$.

A.why: You undid the sum of fractions one term at a time, as if $\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ meant $T = a + b$. You can't flip a sum of reciprocals term by term.

C.why: $\frac{b - T}{bT}$ is $\frac{1}{a}$. You forgot the last step, taking the reciprocal to get $a$.

D.why: You subtracted the fractions in the wrong order and wrote $\frac{T - b}{bT}$ for $\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{b}$. Since $T < b$, your answer is negative, which can't be a number of days.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A public health team models the concentration $C$ of an airborne irritant at a distance of $d$ meters from a source that releases it at a rate $Q$. The constant $k$ depends on ventilation in the room.

$C = \frac{kQ}{d^2}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $C$, $k$, $Q$, and $d$. Which equation correctly expresses $d$ in terms of $C$, $k$, and $Q$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $d^2$ to get $Cd^2 = kQ$, then divide by $C$: $d^2 = \frac{kQ}{C}$. Because $d$ is positive, take the positive square root: $d = \sqrt{\frac{kQ}{C}}$. Check: with $k = 2$, $Q = 50$, $d = 5$, you get $C = 4$, and $\sqrt{\frac{100}{4}} = 5$.

A.why: $\frac{kQ}{C}$ is $d^2$, not $d$. You didn't take the square root at the end.

B.why: You isolated $\frac{1}{d^2} = \frac{C}{kQ}$ and took the square root without first taking the reciprocal. That gives $\frac{1}{d}$, not $d$.

D.why: You took the square root of the numerator only. The root has to apply to the whole quotient $\frac{kQ}{C}$.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A folklorist cataloguing versions of a trickster tale records $n$ versions collected from oral storytellers and $m$ versions found in printed collections. The fraction of all recorded versions that are oral is $V$, where $V < 1$.

$V = \frac{n}{n + m}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $V$, $n$, and $m$. Which equation correctly expresses $n$ in terms of $V$ and $m$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $n + m$: $Vn + Vm = n$. Collect the $n$ terms on one side: $Vm = n - Vn = n(1 - V)$. Divide by $1 - V$: $n = \frac{Vm}{1 - V}$. Check: with $n = 2$ and $m = 6$, $V = 0.25$, and $\frac{0.25 \cdot 6}{0.75} = 2$.

A.why: You collected and factored $n$ correctly but dropped the coefficient $V$ on the $Vm$ term.

B.why: You lost a sign when you collected the $n$ terms. Subtracting $Vn$ from $n$ gives $n(1 - V)$, not $n(1 + V)$.

C.why: You set up $n(1 - V) = Vm$ correctly but divided the wrong way round. That flips the expression you need.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
An agricultural scientist measures the moisture content $M$ of harvested grain on a dry basis. A sample weighs $W$ grams when freshly harvested and $D$ grams after oven drying.

$M = \frac{W - D}{D}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $M$, $W$, and $D$. Which equation correctly expresses $D$ in terms of $M$ and $W$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $D$: $MD = W - D$. Add $D$ to both sides so every $D$ term is on one side: $MD + D = W$, so $D(M + 1) = W$. Divide: $D = \frac{W}{M + 1}$. Check: with $W = 150$ and $D = 100$, $M = 0.5$, and $\frac{150}{1.5} = 100$.

A.why: You dropped a sign when you moved $-D$ across the equals sign. It becomes $+D$, so the factor is $M + 1$, not $M - 1$.

C.why: $\frac{M + 1}{W}$ is $\frac{1}{D}$. You needed one more step: take the reciprocal.

D.why: You reached $D(M + 1) = W$ and then multiplied by $M + 1$ when you should have divided by it. This would make the dry weight bigger than the wet weight.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
A printmaker centres a square linoleum block, $s$ inches on a side, on a square sheet of paper. The sheet leaves a margin of $b$ inches on every side of the block and has an area of $A$ square inches.

$A = (s + 2b)^2$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $A$, $s$, and $b$. Which equation correctly expresses $s$ in terms of $A$ and $b$?
items.explanation: All the lengths are positive, so take the positive square root of both sides: $\sqrt{A} = s + 2b$. Subtract $2b$: $s = \sqrt{A} - 2b$. Check: with $s = 10$ and $b = 2$, $A = 196$, and $\sqrt{196} - 4 = 10$.

B.why: You subtracted $2b$ before taking the square root. The $2b$ is inside the square, so you have to take the root first and then subtract.

C.why: You treated $(s + 2b)^2$ as $s^2 + 4b^2$ and undid it term by term. Squaring a sum also produces the cross term $4sb$, so this doesn't work.

D.why: You took the square root correctly but added $2b$ when you should have subtracted it. That makes the block wider than the sheet.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
On a topographic map, two trail markers are $d$ centimeters apart. Each map centimeter represents $r$ meters on the ground. The higher marker has an elevation of $E$ meters and the lower one an elevation of $e$ meters, and a cartographer computes the average grade $g$ between them.

$g = \frac{E - e}{rd}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $g$, $E$, $e$, $r$, and $d$. Which equation correctly expresses $e$ in terms of $g$, $E$, $r$, and $d$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $rd$: $grd = E - e$. Add $e$ and subtract $grd$: $e = E - grd$. Check: with $E = 500$, $e = 300$, $r = 100$, $d = 4$, you get $g = 0.5$, and $500 - 0.5 \cdot 400 = 300$.

A.why: You dropped a sign while isolating $e$. From $grd = E - e$, you get $e = E - grd$. Your version is the negative of the correct elevation.

B.why: You mixed up terms and factors. You subtracted $g$ as though it were added to $E$, but $g$ is multiplied by $rd$, so you have to clear the denominator first.

C.why: You divided $g$ by $rd$ when you should have multiplied. Clearing the denominator $rd$ means multiplying both sides by it.

items.subtype_name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
items.stimulus:
Paleobotanists estimate past carbon dioxide levels from the stomatal index $I$ of fossil leaves. On a sample of leaf cuticle, $S$ is the number of stomata counted and $E$ is the number of ordinary epidermal cells counted.

$I = \frac{100S}{S + E}$
items.stem: The given equation relates the positive numbers $I$, $S$, and $E$. Which equation correctly expresses $E$ in terms of $I$ and $S$?
items.explanation: Multiply both sides by $S + E$: $IS + IE = 100S$. Subtract $IS$: $IE = 100S - IS = S(100 - I)$. Divide by $I$: $E = \frac{S(100 - I)}{I}$. Check: with $S = 20$ and $E = 80$, $I = 20$, and $\frac{20 \cdot 80}{20} = 80$.

A.why: You dropped a sign when you moved $IS$ to the other side. It leaves $100S - IS$, not $IS - 100S$, so your count comes out negative.

B.why: $\frac{100S}{I}$ equals $S + E$, the total number of cells counted. You still needed to subtract $S$ to get the epidermal cells alone.

D.why: You divided by 100 when you should have divided by the coefficient of $E$, which is $I$.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: The Wage Ledger is a 1911 novel by Marguerite Osler. Its central figure, Hollis Crane, is a clerk at a shipyard where the owners have just lowered the piece rates paid to riveters. Crane's job is to calculate and record each man's earnings under the new rates. In a study of the novel, one scholar argues that Crane privately doubts the fairness of the reduced rates even as he applies them with scrupulous care:
items.stem: Which quotation from The Wage Ledger most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "He entered each reduced rate in his neatest hand, pausing only to wonder whether the men who earned it could live on it."
"Crane had never once miscounted a riveter's wage, and the owners trusted his ledger far above their own accounts."
"The new rates struck him as a cruelty, and at night he lay awake composing protests he knew he would never send."
"Crane refused to enter the new rates, telling the foreman that no honest clerk could put his name to such figures."
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Crane doubts that the lower rates are fair, and he still applies them carefully. In this line he writes each reduced rate "in his neatest hand," which shows the care, and he wonders whether the men "could live on it," which shows the doubt. No other choice shows both.

C.why: This is the same trap from the other side. Crane clearly thinks the rates are cruel, but nothing here shows him actually applying them, let alone carefully. You matched the emotion and missed the action the claim requires.

D.why: Here Crane refuses to apply the rates at all. The claim says he applies them with scrupulous care, so this line reverses his behaviour.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: "Plate and Acid" is a 1934 poem by Ines Harrow, who worked as an etcher. In etching, an artist scratches lines through a waxy coating on a copper plate, and an acid bath then bites those lines permanently into the metal. Critics have noted that the poem is less interested in the lines the etcher plans than in the ones she doesn't. According to one critic, the speaker treats the accidental marks the acid preserves as permanent and also as something she values:
items.stem: Which quotation from "Plate and Acid" most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "I draw the needle slowly through the ground, / and every line obeys the hand that made it."
"The slip the acid kept, I keep as well; / by morning it is what the print is for."
"The stray scratch deepened overnight; I scraped / the copper smooth and started it again."
"No stroke, once bitten, ever can be called back; / the plate remembers what the hand forgot."
items.explanation: The claim is about accidental marks, and it says two things about them: they are permanent, and the speaker values them. "The slip the acid kept" is an accident made permanent, and "I keep as well... it is what the print is for" shows she treasures it. Only this line shows both.

A.why: These are deliberate lines that "obey the hand." The claim is about accidental marks, so this line is on the right topic but describes the opposite kind of line.

C.why: The speaker erases the stray scratch and starts over. That treats the accident as unwanted and as something she can undo, which goes against both parts of the claim.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. "What the hand forgot" does suggest an accident made permanent, so the line gets the first half right. But it says nothing about the speaker valuing the mark, and the claim needs both.

items.subtype_name: Pick the line from the literary work that illustrates the claim
items.stimulus: Notes on the Weather of the Fen Country is an 1868 book by Josiah Marle, a farmer who kept a daily weather record for more than thirty years. At the time, London newspapers had just begun printing national forecasts. Historians of meteorology value Marle's book for its candour. One historian observes that Marle preferred his own local signs to the published forecasts, though he never hid the times his own signs failed him:
items.stem: Which quotation from Notes on the Weather of the Fen Country most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: "The printed forecasts from London are of little use to a man in the fens, and I have long since ceased to read them."
"On the ninth I foretold rain from the low swallows, and the day was dry; I set it down so that I might not forget it."
"I would sooner trust the swallows than the London papers, though the swallows have misled me thrice this summer."
"The London forecasts proved truer than my swallows this summer, and I now consult them before I sow a field."
items.explanation: The claim needs two things: Marle prefers his local signs to the published forecasts, and he admits when those signs fail. This line ranks the swallows above the London papers and also admits they "misled me thrice this summer." It is the only choice that does both.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. Marle rejects the London forecasts, which covers his preference, but he never admits that his own signs fail. It shows only half of the claim.

B.why: Marle honestly records a failed prediction here, but the published forecasts never come up, so the line doesn't show that he preferred his own signs to them. You matched the candour and missed the comparison.

D.why: Here Marle trusts the London forecasts over his own signs. The claim says he preferred his own signs, so this reverses the comparison.

items.stimulus: The Buried Terrace is a 1952 novel by Rosalind Achterberg. It follows the archaeologist Nell Varga through a season spent excavating a hillside villa, where every bucket of soil must be passed through a fine sieve so that small finds are not lost. "Varga paced the trench edge each afternoon, cursing the sieves that took an hour to fill with nothing."

FENN: "I have read every paper on rickets this decade, and I believe the answer lies in cod-liver oil."

D.why: This line comes from the right world of nutrition research but is about a different subject, his theory about rickets. It says nothing about measuring meals or about uneaten food.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Seismologists have generally regarded slow slip events, in which a fault creeps for weeks without producing noticeable shaking, as a kind of safety valve: by releasing built-up stress gradually, they were thought to lower the odds of a large earthquake. However, seismologist Mereana Tuhi's analysis of the Hikurangi margin off New Zealand found that several slow slip events shifted stress onto neighboring locked sections of the fault, where swarms of small earthquakes followed. Tuhi notes that her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, but she argues that slow slip should no longer be viewed simply as a release of danger.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Swarms of small earthquakes occurred on locked sections of the Hikurangi margin after several slow slip events.
Slow slip events release stress so gradually that small earthquakes seldom follow them along the Hikurangi margin.
Evidence that slow slip events can shift stress to nearby fault sections challenges the view that they simply reduce earthquake risk.
Tuhi's analysis demonstrates that slow slip events make major earthquakes more likely on neighboring fault sections.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the accepted view that slow slip is a safety valve. After 'However,' it brings in Tuhi's finding that slow slip can move stress onto neighboring sections, and it ends with her argument that the old view is too simple. Choice C covers the expected view, the finding and the conclusion without claiming more than Tuhi does.

A.why: You picked a detail that is accurate but only one step in the argument. The swarms are evidence. The passage uses them to challenge an assumption, and this choice leaves that challenge out.

B.why: You probably recognised 'release stress' from the opening and stopped reading. The passage says swarms of small earthquakes did follow slow slip, which is the opposite of 'seldom follow.'

D.why: You missed the hedge. Tuhi explicitly says her data cannot show whether major quakes become more likely, so 'demonstrates' claims something she refuses to claim.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Fossil leaves record not only which plants once grew in a place but also the climate they grew in. Among living woody plants, species with smooth leaf edges are more common in warm regions, while toothed edges predominate in cool ones. For example, when paleobotanist Ines Varga examined a 52-million-year-old leaf bed in the Dunmore Formation, she found that only about a fifth of its species had toothed edges, pointing to a warm climate. That estimate closely matched temperatures inferred independently from chemical signatures in nearby marine sediments.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Only about a fifth of the species in the Dunmore Formation leaf bed had leaves with toothed edges.
The shapes of fossil leaves can provide evidence about ancient climates, as Varga's study of one leaf bed illustrates.
Leaf shape gives more accurate estimates of ancient temperatures than chemical signatures in marine sediments do.
Fossil leaf beds reveal much about which plants once grew in a place but little about the climates of the past.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes the general claim that fossil leaves record climate. Everything after 'For example' is one case that supports it. Choice B states the general claim and ties Varga's study to it, so it covers the whole passage.

A.why: You chose a statistic from the example. It is correct, but it is there only to support the opening claim about what fossil leaves can reveal.

C.why: You read a ranking into the passage. The two estimates 'closely matched,' and the text never says leaf shape is more accurate than the sediment chemistry.

D.why: The first half of this choice matches the opening, but the second half reverses it. The passage's point is that fossil leaves reveal climate as well as plants.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Immunologists have traditionally divided the immune system into two branches: an adaptive branch that remembers specific pathogens and an innate branch that responds to every threat as if meeting it for the first time. Recent studies suggest this division may be too tidy. After people receive certain vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine for tuberculosis, their monocytes, a type of innate immune cell, can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months. The effect appears briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, but it suggests the innate branch may be capable of a limited kind of memory.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: After BCG vaccination, monocytes can respond more vigorously to unrelated microbes for several months.
Innate immune cells appear to remember specific pathogens as durably and precisely as adaptive cells do.
Vaccines such as BCG can protect people against nearly any microbe by strengthening their innate immune cells.
The innate immune branch, long thought to lack memory, may possess a limited and less targeted form of it.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the traditional split, says it 'may be too tidy,' gives the BCG evidence, and ends with a hedged conclusion that innate cells may have a limited memory. Choice D keeps both the claim and its limits: 'may' and 'limited and less targeted.'

A.why: You chose the evidence instead of what it shows. The monocyte finding is accurate, but the passage uses it to question how immunologists divide the immune system.

B.why: You kept 'innate cells remember' and dropped the qualification. The passage says the effect is briefer and far less targeted than adaptive memory, not equally durable and precise.

C.why: You stretched the finding into a big claim about protection. The text reports stronger responses to some unrelated microbes for months. It never says people are protected against nearly any microbe.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Print collectors have long prized the earliest impressions from a run, assuming that later ones show a block worn down by repeated pressing. The linocuts of Hedda Lorne, a printmaker active in the 1920s, complicate that assumption. Lorne regularly recut her blocks between printings, adding figures and deepening shadows, and she adjusted her inks from one batch to the next. In letters, she called her late impressions 'the finished picture.' For Lorne's work, then, a later impression may be not a degraded copy but the version she most intended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: For Lorne's linocuts, later impressions may represent the artist's intended work rather than inferior copies.
Lorne adjusted the inks she used for her linocuts from one batch of impressions to the next.
Later impressions of prints are generally more valuable than early ones, as Lorne's letters demonstrate.
Lorne's linocuts confirm that early impressions preserve details that are lost as a block wears down.
items.explanation: The middle sentences give separate facts: the recut blocks, the changed inks and the letters. The final sentence, which opens with 'then,' combines them into one verdict. Choice A restates that verdict with its limits intact: it applies to Lorne's work, and it says 'may.'

C.why: You widened a claim about one artist to prints in general and added a claim about value that the passage never makes.

D.why: This repeats the collectors' assumption that the passage says Lorne's work complicates. Her prints challenge that view instead of confirming it.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Dietary guidelines usually treat fiber as a single nutrient, recommending a daily total in grams. However, research led by nutrition scientist Priya Anand suggests that total may be only part of the story. Different fibers feed different gut bacteria, and in Anand's trial, an inulin supplement sharply raised levels of beneficial Bifidobacterium in most participants but barely changed them in others, depending on which microbes each person already carried. Anand concludes that fiber's effects likely depend on both the kind of fiber and the eater's existing gut community.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In Anand's trial, an inulin supplement raised levels of Bifidobacterium in most of the participants.
Fiber supplements do not benefit people whose gut bacteria differ from those of most other people.
Fiber's effects may depend on the type of fiber and a person's gut microbes, not only on the total eaten.
Anand's research confirms that all types of fiber affect the gut's bacteria in much the same way.
items.explanation: After 'However,' the passage argues that a daily total is only part of the story, and Anand's conclusion names the two factors that also matter. Choice C gives both factors, contrasts them with the single-total view, and keeps the hedge.

A.why: You chose half of one trial result. It leaves out the participants who barely changed, and that variation is the point the passage is making.

B.why: You turned 'barely changed' Bifidobacterium levels in some people into 'no benefit' for a whole group. The passage never measures overall benefit and never makes that claim.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the decade after beavers were reintroduced to a river in the Scottish Borders, surveys recorded a marked rise in the number of dragonfly species along its banks. Ecologist Callum Reid considers it plausible that the beavers were responsible, since their dams create the still, plant-rich ponds in which many dragonfly larvae thrive. Establishing the beavers' role, Reid argues, will require comparing this river with similar ones where beavers are absent.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Beavers may explain the river's rise in dragonfly species, but confirming this requires further comparison.
New limits on fertilizer runoff from nearby farms took effect during the decade after beavers returned.
Reid argues that reduced fertilizer runoff, not beaver ponds, explains the rise in dragonfly species.
items.explanation: Reid grants that the beaver explanation is plausible, points out a competing cause, and says more comparison is needed. Choice B matches that structure: a limited concession ('may') followed by the call for more evidence.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Refuse heaps, or middens, were once excavated mainly for the intact objects that might be buried in them. Middens reveal more about ancient societies than any other kind of archaeological evidence does.
Middens are valued by archaeologists mainly because they preserve intact objects such as loom weights.
Archaeologists now study middens as records of changing daily life, as a study at Tel Harun illustrates.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The 1914 anthology Songs of the Northern Dales has always been credited to the collector Albert Fenwick, whose name alone appears on its title page. However, Fenwick's field notebooks, recently catalogued by musicologist Dana Okafor, tell a different story. Most of the transcriptions in them are in the hand of his assistant, Mabel Hurst, and notes in the margins show Hurst insisting on preserving singers' irregular rhythms, which Fenwick had wanted to smooth out. Hurst insisted on preserving the irregular rhythms of singers, which Fenwick had wanted to smooth out.
Fenwick's notebooks show that he transcribed most of the songs himself before later crediting Hurst.
Most early folk-song anthologies were largely compiled by assistants whose work went uncredited.
items.explanation: The passage opens with the official credit to Fenwick. After 'However,' the notebooks show Hurst's hand and her editorial choices, and Okafor concludes that Hurst shaped the anthology as much as Fenwick did. Choice A captures that correction to the credit.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: For decades, sprint coaches prescribed long, held stretches before races, reasoning that looser muscles would move faster. Physiologist Dana Okafor tested that reasoning with thirty collegiate sprinters, who ran 40-meter dashes after either five minutes of held stretches or five minutes of leg swings and skips. The results, however, ran counter to the coaches' expectation: the sprinters were, on average, slightly slower after the held stretches. Okafor suggests that holding a stretch may briefly reduce a muscle's springiness, the very quality a sprint start depends on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Okafor's study compared two five-minute warm-up routines, using thirty collegiate sprinters as its participants.
A study suggests that the held stretches coaches long recommended before sprints may slightly slow sprinters down.
Okafor's study shows that athletes should remove stretching of every kind from their training programs.
Okafor found that held stretches improved sprint times by making the sprinters' leg muscles springier.
items.explanation: The passage sets up the coaches' long-held belief, then uses 'however' to bring in the real finding: held stretches were followed by slightly slower sprints, possibly because they reduce springiness. Choice B covers both the belief and the finding that corrects it, and it keeps the text's hedge ('may').

A.why: This accurately describes how the study was set up, but it leaves out what the study found. You picked a true detail from the middle of the passage instead of the point the whole passage is building toward.

C.why: The study only compared held stretches with leg swings and skips before sprints. It says nothing about getting rid of all stretching, and leg swings are themselves a kind of dynamic stretching. You stretched a narrow finding into a sweeping rule.

D.why: The sprinters were slower after held stretches, and Okafor suggests that stretching reduces springiness. This choice turns both parts of the finding around, so you may have taken the coaches' expectation for the result.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Leaves and wood fossilize only under unusual conditions, so many ancient plants are missing from the record of large fossils. Pollen grains, by contrast, have tough outer walls that survive in ordinary lake mud. At the Harlow Basin site, for instance, paleobotanist Mei Tanaka found abundant pollen from a flowering shrub in 52-million-year-old sediments, though not a single leaf of that shrub has been found anywhere in the basin. Pollen analysis has made the study of fossil leaves and wood unnecessary for understanding ancient plants.
Pollen grains are fragile, so they survive only in the unusual conditions that also preserve fossil leaves.
Because pollen survives more readily than leaves and wood, it can reveal ancient plants that large fossils miss.
items.explanation: The first two sentences make a general claim: large plant fossils are rare, but pollen survives well. The Harlow Basin case is an example of that claim, and the final sentence says the pollen fills the gap. Choice D states the general claim that the example supports.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Some meteorologists have proposed that the heat radiating from large cities may trigger summer thunderstorms downwind. Radar records from the city of Aldermoor appear to fit this idea: storms form noticeably more often just east of the city than to its west. Meteorologist Priya Venkatesan cautions, however, that the prevailing winds also carry moisture from nearby Lake Tessel over the same eastern area. The lake, rather than the city's heat, could therefore account for the pattern, and separating the two influences will require further study.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Radar records fit the idea that city heat triggers storms downwind, but moisture from a lake could also explain them.
Radar records prove that Aldermoor's heat is the main reason summer storms form more often east of the city.
Prevailing summer winds near Aldermoor carry moisture from Lake Tessel over the area east of the city.
Venkatesan rejects the heat hypothesis because storms east of Aldermoor are no more common than elsewhere.
items.explanation: The passage gives a hypothesis and some evidence that fits it, then uses 'however' to bring in a second possible explanation, and ends by saying more study is needed. Choice A covers both the fit and the doubt, and like the text it does not claim certainty.

B.why: The passage says the records 'appear to fit' the idea, and then raises a competing explanation. 'Prove' and 'main reason' are much stronger than the text allows. You missed the hedge words.

C.why: This detail is accurate, but it is only one step in the passage's argument. It does not mention the heat hypothesis or the uncertainty the passage is really about.

D.why: The records show storms do form more often east of the city. Venkatesan does not reject the hypothesis either. She only says another cause is possible.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists generally expect a large new employer to push up wages in a small town by competing for workers. Examining warehouse openings in forty rural counties, economist Luis Ferreira found that hourly pay at nearby retailers did rise, by about 4 percent in the first year. Many retail workers soon moved to the warehouses, though, and retailers responded by cutting staff and hours rather than raising pay further. Within three years, retail wages had drifted back close to their earlier levels. Taken together, Ferreira's findings suggest that the wage boost from a new large employer may be real but short-lived.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In the first year after a warehouse opened nearby, hourly pay at local retailers rose by about 4 percent.
Opening a large warehouse is the most effective way for a rural county to raise its long-term wages.
Research suggests that a large new employer may raise local wages at first, but the increase may not last.
Retail wages kept climbing for three years after the warehouses opened, as competition for workers grew.
items.explanation: The middle sentences give separate facts: an early rise, workers leaving retail jobs, and wages falling back. The last sentence adds them up: the boost is 'real but short-lived.' Choice C restates that conclusion and keeps its hedge.

B.why: The passage finds that the wage gain faded, and it never compares warehouses with other ways of raising wages. 'Most effective' and 'long-term' are claims the text does not support.

items.stimulus: Farmers across the Venn Plateau widely credit a drought-tolerant maize variety, introduced in 2015, for the sharp rise in local yields since then. However, when agronomist Hana Brisco compared records from 300 farms, she found that yields rose just as much on farms that kept planting older varieties. items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The loss of a single predator can reshape an entire ecosystem. Consider Lake Corvin, where heavy angling during the 1990s removed most of the largemouth bass. Freed from their chief predator, small minnows multiplied rapidly. The minnows, in turn, consumed much of the lake's zooplankton, the tiny animals that had kept algae in check. As the case of Lake Corvin shows, losing one predator can set off a chain of changes across an ecosystem.

B.why: The passage describes one lake. It never compares causes of algae blooms or makes a claim about lakes worldwide. You turned a single example into a global ranking.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the mountain village of Ostrava Alta, residents can hold conversations entirely in whistles. Linguist Tomás Reyna has proposed that this whistled speech arose so that shepherds could talk across steep valleys, and his recordings show that the whistles carry about two kilometers, far beyond the reach of shouted words. Yet, as other researchers point out, showing that the system works well over distance does not show why it began. It may have started as a courtship code or a children's game and only later been put to use across the valleys.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Recordings show that the whistled speech of Ostrava Alta carries about two kilometers across the valleys.
The whistles' long range shows that they are useful over distance, but not that this is why they began.
The whistles' long range proves that villagers first developed them to speak across the steep valleys.
Shouted words carry farther than whistles, so the whistled speech most likely began as a children's game.
items.explanation: The passage grants that the whistles carry far, then uses 'Yet' to raise the stronger objection: being useful over distance does not explain how the system began. Choice B keeps both the concession and the limit.

The following text is from Tomasz Reyna's 2008 poem "Proof." The speaker is a printmaker.

All morning I cut the block by feel,
gouging the pale wood toward a shape
I carried backward in my head.
I rolled the ink, black and slow as tar,
laid the paper, leaned my weight on it.

did I see what my hands had meant—
the heron, facing the right way at last,
more certain than I ever was.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

The speaker is frustrated that the finished print differs from the image planned.
The speaker works without fully seeing the image until the finished print reveals it.
The speaker regrets choosing a medium that offers so little certainty to the artist.

To celebrate the speaker's discovery of living ferns growing in a ravine
To explain how ferns came to be preserved in shale over long periods
To reassure the fern that its kind has endured despite its own apparent loss

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Hollis Arden's 2017 poem "To a First-Year Grower." The speaker addresses a new farmer.

You will want the seed to hurry.
Everyone does. The first spring,
you'll kneel each dawn to check the rows
as if watching could pull green from clay.
It can't. But here is what I learned
from forty harvests of beans and doubt:
the waiting is not wasted. Under you,
the roots are doing arithmetic
you cannot see, and by July
the field will show its work.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To warn a new grower that checking the rows too often will damage the young crop
To lament the many seasons the speaker spent doubting whether the beans would grow
To encourage a new grower to trust that growth is happening even when it is unseen
To explain the process by which bean roots draw nutrients out of heavy clay soil
items.explanation: The poem speaks to the new grower. It admits that impatience is natural, and then after 'But' comes the real message: 'the waiting is not wasted,' because the roots are working out of sight and 'by July / the field will show its work.' The tone is reassuring, so the purpose is to encourage the grower to trust growth they can't see yet.

A.why: You turned encouragement into a warning. The speaker says watching can't speed the crop up. The poem never says watching harms it.

B.why: 'Forty harvests of beans and doubt' is the speaker's credential, not a lament. The poem looks ahead with hope, so this choice gets the tone backward.

D.why: 'The roots are doing arithmetic' is a metaphor. The poem never explains how roots take up nutrients, so you've credited it with content it doesn't have.

The following text is adapted from Oona Maris's 2016 short story "The Eyepiece." Teodor is an amateur astronomer.

To explain the procedure seismologists follow to find an epicenter and estimate magnitude

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Ansel Burke's 2021 poem "For the Volunteers Pulling Buckthorn." The speaker addresses people removing an invasive shrub from a forest.

You will not see the oak you're making room for.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To encourage the volunteers to keep working even though they may never see the results
To warn the volunteers that invasive plants will likely return to the cleared hillside
To lament that the volunteers will move away before the restored forest can mature
To explain why buckthorn outcompetes native plants such as oak and trillium on hillsides
items.explanation: The speaker addresses the volunteers and admits the hard parts: they won't see the oak, the work is exhausting, and the pile looks small. C.why: The poem does mention that the volunteers will move away, but only as a reason to 'pull anyway.' Reading it as a lament gets the tone wrong.

D.why: The poem names oak and trillium but never explains how buckthorn competes with them. You've read ecological reasoning into it that isn't there.

items.stimulus: Hydrologists call a river a "losing stream" when it feeds water into the ground beneath it instead of drawing water from it. items.stimulus: For decades, the fossil plant Velatophyllum, known only from scattered leaf impressions in Antarctic rock, was assumed to be a fern. However, specimens recovered in 2019 preserve small seeds attached to the leaf bases, and ferns reproduce by spores, not seeds. Those seeds have thick protective coats, and the plant's leaves grew in tight, leathery clusters. Together, these features have led paleobotanists to reclassify Velatophyllum as an early seed plant, one apparently suited to surviving long, dark polar winters.

choices: To explain why ferns reproduce by spores rather than by producing seeds on their leaves
To argue that most plant fossils found in Antarctica have been misidentified by researchers
To describe how new specimens changed scientists' view of what kind of plant a fossil was
To show that the 2019 specimens confirmed that Velatophyllum was an unusual kind of fern
items.explanation: The text opens with a long-held assumption that Velatophyllum was a fern, turns on 'However' to the 2019 seed-bearing specimens, and ends with the plant's reclassification. Choice C covers that old-view-to-new-view structure for the fossil as a whole.

A.why: You picked a supporting fact. The point about spores is there only to show why seeds rule out a fern. It is a step in the reasoning, not the text's purpose.

B.why: You generalized beyond the text. It discusses one misidentified fossil and says nothing about most Antarctic plant fossils, and it doesn't argue a broad claim.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. The 2019 specimens overturned the fern classification rather than confirming it, and Velatophyllum was reclassified as a seed plant.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
items.stimulus: Metallic glasses are alloys cooled so quickly that their atoms freeze in a disordered arrangement instead of forming crystals, which makes them unusually strong and springy. For decades, however, they could be produced only as thin ribbons or small pieces, because thicker samples cooled too slowly at their centers and crystallized. Engineer Hana Okafor's team has now developed an iron-based alloy that stays glassy at thicknesses of several centimeters. Its first commercial use, in springs for precision watches, exploits the material's ability to flex millions of times without permanently deforming.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain why rapid cooling keeps the atoms in certain alloys from arranging into crystals
To argue that metallic glasses will soon replace steel in most kinds of industrial manufacturing

items.stimulus: In some languages, a speaker cannot simply report that something happened; the grammar itself requires the speaker to indicate how they know it. Linguists call this feature evidentiality. In Tamuri, a language spoken by about 12,000 people in the Andean highlands, one verb suffix marks events the speaker witnessed, another marks events learned from others, and a third marks conclusions drawn from clues, such as wet ground indicating rain. Leaving the suffix off is not an option: a Tamuri sentence without one is ungrammatical.

To show that Tamuri speakers may decide for themselves whether to mark their sources

items.stimulus: Ecologists have traditionally assumed that earthworms in northern hardwood forests benefit tree seedlings by speeding the release of nutrients from fallen leaves. To test this assumption, ecologist Mireille Okafor fenced forty forest plots, removed the worms from half of them, and tracked sugar maple seedlings in every plot for three years. To argue that earthworms should be removed from northern hardwood forests in order to protect seedlings

items.stimulus: Most earthquakes release built-up stress within seconds. Along some subduction zones, however, the boundary between two plates can slip over weeks without producing strong shaking. In these slow slip events, fluids squeezed out of the descending plate collect along the fault and reduce the friction that normally locks the plates together. The plates then creep past each other a few centimeters at a time, and that movement can transfer stress to neighboring, still-locked segments of the fault, which may later rupture in ordinary earthquakes.

To question the view that slow slip events can add stress to neighboring segments of a fault

items.stimulus: Hydrologists have long relied on rainfall totals to forecast floods, but in mountain basins during winter, rain alone can be a poor guide. items.stimulus: Many songbirds that migrate in autumn must cross hundreds of kilometers of open water without stopping. In the weeks before departure, such a bird enters a phase of intense feeding, eating almost constantly and converting much of the food into fat stored beneath its skin. To argue that songbirds whose organs shrink the most are the likeliest to survive their migration

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A linguist models how many distinct word forms appear in a growing transcript of an endangered language. The model uses the equation $3(x + 4)(2x - 5) = ax^2 + bx + c$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, what is the value of $a + b + c$?
items.explanation: First expand the product: $(x + 4)(2x - 5) = 2x^2 + 3x - 20$. Then multiply every term by 3 to get $6x^2 + 9x - 60$. So $a = 6$, $b = 9$, and $c = -60$, which gives $a + b + c = 6 + 9 - 60 = -45$. To check, put $x = 1$ into the left side: $3(5)(-3) = -45$.

A.why: You found $c = -60$ and stopped there. The question asks for the sum $a + b + c$, not the constant term alone.

C.why: You expanded $(x + 4)(2x - 5)$ but never multiplied by the 3 in front, so you added the coefficients of $2x^2 + 3x - 20$. The 3 multiplies the whole expression.

D.why: You made a sign error in the middle term and got $-3x$ instead of $+3x$ ($-5x + 8x = 3x$). That gave $6x^2 - 9x - 60$.

items.explanation: Match the leading coefficients: $2a = 10$, so $a = 5$. Match the constant terms: $3b = -12$, so $b = -4$. Check with the $x$-term: $ab + 6 = -20 + 6 = -14$, which matches. So $ab = 5(-4) = -20$.

C.why: You dropped the negative sign when solving $3b = -12$ and used $b = 4$. With that value the $x$-term would be $+26x$, not $-14x$.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A public health analyst fits a curve to weekly clinic visits during a flu season and rewrites it in vertex form: $2x^2 + 12x + 23 = a(x + h)^2 + k$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $h$, and $k$ are constants, what is the value of $a + h + k$?
items.explanation: Factor 2 out of the $x$-terms: $2(x^2 + 6x) + 23$. Completing the square inside the parentheses gives $2[(x + 3)^2 - 9] + 23$. The 2 multiplies the $-9$ as well, so this becomes $2(x + 3)^2 - 18 + 23 = 2(x + 3)^2 + 5$. So $a = 2$, $h = 3$, and $k = 5$, and $a + h + k = 10$.

B.why: You found $h = 3$ and $k = 5$ but left $a$ out of the sum. The question asks for all three constants.

C.why: You subtracted 9 instead of $2 \cdot 9 = 18$, so you got $k = 14$. The factor of 2 multiplies everything inside the brackets, including the $-9$.

D.why: You took $h = -3$ because the vertex is at $x = -3$. In the form $(x + h)^2$, the expression $(x + 3)^2$ means $h = +3$.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: An astronomer compares two models of the brightness of a variable star. The difference between the models is written as $(3x - 2)^2 - (x + 4)^2 = ax^2 + bx + c$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, what is the value of $a + b + c$?
items.explanation: Expand each square: $(3x - 2)^2 = 9x^2 - 12x + 4$ and $(x + 4)^2 = x^2 + 8x + 16$. Subtract all three terms of the second square: $9x^2 - 12x + 4 - x^2 - 8x - 16 = 8x^2 - 20x - 12$. So $a + b + c = 8 - 20 - 12 = -24$. To check, put $x = 1$ into the left side: $1 - 25 = -24$.

B.why: You found $c = -12$ and stopped. The question asks for $a + b + c$.

D.why: You squared each binomial as the sum of two squares, for example $(3x - 2)^2 = 9x^2 + 4$, and left out the middle terms.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A seismologist models how ground displacement decays after a tremor. The model uses the equation $(x - 3)(x^2 + kx + 4) = x^3 - x^2 + px - 12$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $k$ and $p$ are constants, what is the value of $k + p$?
items.explanation: Expanding gives $x^3 + (k - 3)x^2 + (4 - 3k)x - 12$. Match the $x^2$ terms: $k - 3 = -1$, so $k = 2$. Match the $x$-terms: $p = 4 - 3(2) = -2$. So $k + p = 2 + (-2) = 0$.

A.why: You found $k = 2$ and stopped. You still need $p$, and then the sum $k + p$.

D.why: You solved $k - 3 = -1$ by subtracting 3 and got $k = -4$, which then gave $p = 16$. Add 3 to both sides instead, so $k = 2$.

items.stimulus: A meteorologist models the change in air pressure along a cold front. The model uses the equation $5(x - 1)(x + 3) - 2(x + 4) = ax^2 + bx + c$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, what is the value of $a - b + c$?
items.explanation: First, $(x - 1)(x + 3) = x^2 + 2x - 3$. Multiply each term by 5 to get $5x^2 + 10x - 15$. Then subtract $2x + 8$ to get $5x^2 + 8x - 23$. So $a - b + c = 5 - 8 - 23 = -26$. To check, put $x = -1$ into the left side: $5(-2)(2) - 2(3) = -26$.

A.why: You computed $a + b + c$, the value at $x = 1$. The question asks for $a - b + c$, which needs the minus sign on $b$.

B.why: You found $c = -23$ and stopped. You still need to combine it with $a$ and $b$ as the question asks.

C.why: You multiplied only the $x^2$ term by 5 and wrote $5x^2 + 2x - 3$. The 5 multiplies every term of the product.

items.subtype_name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
items.stimulus: A musicologist models how the tempo of a recorded performance drifts over time. The model uses the equation $(x^2 + 3)(ax - 2) + 4x = 5x^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$.
items.stem: If the given equation is true for all values of $x$, where $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ are constants, what is the value of $c + d$?
items.explanation: Expanding gives $ax^3 - 2x^2 + 3ax - 6 + 4x$. Match the $x^3$ terms: $a = 5$. The $x$-coefficient is $c = 3a + 4 = 19$, and the constant term is $d = -6$. So $c + d = 19 - 6 = 13$.

A.why: You found $c = 19$ and stopped. The question asks for $c + d$, and $d = -6$.

B.why: You left out the $+4x$ outside the product, so you got $c = 15$. Every $x$-term on the left side adds to $c$.

D.why: You took the $x$-term from $3 \cdot ax$ as $3x$ and dropped the $a$, so you got $c = 7$. Since $a = 5$, that term is $15x$.

items.subtype_name: The sentence needs a real (finite) verb
items.stimulus: In the eighteenth century, silk weavers in London's Spitalfields district produced fabrics of remarkable complexity, using pattern-weaving techniques that refugee artisans had carried with them from France. Few of the designers' working materials survive. One pattern book from the period, now preserved in a museum archive, ______ more than two hundred hand-painted designs for brocaded silk, each annotated with notes on thread colors.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is "One pattern book," and it has no main verb yet. The phrase "now preserved in a museum archive" is only an interrupter. You need a finite verb, and "contains" is the only tensed form. It gives the sentence its main verb and agrees with the singular subject.

A.why: "Containing" sounds smooth, but an -ing form can't be the main verb of a clause. With it, "One pattern book" never gets a verb, and the sentence becomes a fragment.

B.why: "To contain" is an infinitive. It can't be a main verb, so the subject "One pattern book" is left without a predicate.

D.why: "Having contained" is a participle phrase, not a tensed verb. The sentence still has no main verb, and the perfect form clashes with a book that holds these designs now.

items.stimulus: Before satellite imagery existed, mapmakers charted coastlines through a painstaking process called triangulation. On one nineteenth-century survey of a rocky northern shoreline, the field team first measured a single baseline across a flat stretch of beach with steel chains and ______ the angles from each end of that line to distant church towers and hilltops.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The word "and" joins two actions done by the same subject, "the field team." The first action is "measured," a simple past verb. The second action has to be parallel with it, so the answer is "recorded."

B.why: "Recording" is an -ing form. After "and," it doesn't match "measured," so the compound predicate is broken. You probably picked the form that sounded most fluent.

C.why: "To record" is an infinitive. It can't serve as the second verb in a compound predicate that begins with the past-tense verb "measured."

D.why: "Having recorded" is a participle, not a finite verb. It doesn't match "measured," and it suggests the recording happened before the measuring.

items.stimulus: An agronomist transplants a sorghum seedling into a test plot. At the moment it is transplanted, the seedling is 4 centimeters tall. It then grows 2 centimeters each week.
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $h$ is the height, in centimeters, of the seedling $w$ weeks after it is transplanted?
items.explanation: The height at week 0 is 4 cm, so 4 is the constant term. The seedling gains 2 cm per week, so the rate is +2. That gives $h = 2w + 4$.

C.why: You added the starting height and the weekly growth to get 6 and used that as the rate. The 4 cm is there only once, at the start. It is not added again every week.

D.why: You gave the starting height a negative sign. The seedling is 4 cm tall at week 0, so the constant must be +4, not −4.

items.stimulus: At the start of a workday, a field laboratory at an archaeological dig holds 240 unsorted pottery shards. The lab team sorts the shards at a steady rate of 15 shards per hour, and no new shards arrive during the day.
items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $s$ is the number of unsorted shards remaining $t$ hours after the start of the day?
items.explanation: There are 240 unsorted shards when $t = 0$, so 240 is the constant. The pile shrinks by 15 each hour, so the rate is −15. That gives $s = 240 - 15t$.

A.why: You used + for a quantity that is going down. Sorting removes shards from the unsorted pile, so the rate has to be negative.

B.why: You swapped the starting value and the rate. This equation starts with 15 shards and loses 240 per hour.

D.why: You subtracted 15 from 240 once and then used the result as a per-hour rate. After one hour 225 shards are left, but that number is not a rate.

items.stem: Which equation represents this situation, where $n$ is the number of sea stars counted on the first survey?
items.explanation: The second survey is "8 fewer than 3 times" $n$, so you triple $n$ first and then subtract 8, which gives $3n - 8$. The total is the first survey plus the second survey: $n + (3n - 8) = 92$. As a check, $n = 25$ gives $25 + 67 = 92$.

D.why: You reversed the subtraction. "8 fewer than $3n$" means $3n - 8$, not $8 - 3n$.

items.subtype_name: Multi-step angle chase through a composite figure
items.stimulus: A paleobotanist draws two parallel veins in a fossil leaf as lines $\ell$ and $m$. Point $A$ lies on line $\ell$. Points $B$ and $C$ lie on line $m$, with $B$ to the left of $C$. items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ACD$?
items.explanation: Angles $PAB$ and $ABC$ are alternate interior angles formed by the parallel lines and transversal $AB$, so angle $ABC$ is $58^\circ$. In triangle $ABC$, angle $ACB = 180 - 58 - 75 = 47^\circ$. Angle $ACD$ forms a linear pair with angle $ACB$, so it measures $180 - 47 = 133^\circ$. You can check this with the exterior angle rule: $58 + 75 = 133$.

A.why: You found the interior angle $ACB$ of the triangle and stopped. Angle $ACD$ is the exterior angle beside it, so you still need to subtract from 180.

B.why: This is angle $ABC$, the alternate interior partner of angle $PAB$. It is at vertex $B$, not at vertex $C$, where the question asks.

C.why: You found the exterior angle at $B$ ($180 - 58$) when the question asks for the exterior angle at $C$.

items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $AED$?
items.explanation: The $128^\circ$ angle forms a linear pair with angle $EDB$, so angle $EDB = 52^\circ$. Because $\ell \parallel m$ and street $p$ is a transversal, angle $EBD$ is the alternate interior angle to angle $CAE$, so it is $63^\circ$. In triangle $BED$, angle $BED = 180 - 63 - 52 = 65^\circ$. Points $A$, $E$, and $B$ are on one line, so angle $AED = 180 - 65 = 115^\circ$.

A.why: This is angle $EDB$, the supplement of the given $128^\circ$. It is the first link in the chain, not the angle at $E$.

B.why: This is angle $BED$, the interior angle of the triangle at $E$, which also equals its vertical angle $AEC$. Angle $AED$ is the angle supplementary to it.

D.why: This is $180 - 63$, the obtuse angle street $p$ makes with avenue $\ell$ at $A$. It is at the wrong vertex.

items.subtype_name: Multi-step angle chase through a composite figure
items.stimulus: A meteorologist outlines a wedge of cold air on a weather map as triangle $PQR$. Point $S$ lies on side $QR$ between $Q$ and $R$, and segment $PS$ is drawn so that $QS = PS$. The measure of angle $QPR$ is $94^\circ$, and the measure of angle $PRQ$ is $44^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $PSR$?
items.explanation: In triangle $PQR$, angle $PQR = 180 - 94 - 44 = 42^\circ$. Since $QS = PS$, triangle $PQS$ is isosceles with equal base angles, so angle $QPS$ is also $42^\circ$. Angle $PSR$ is an exterior angle of triangle $PQS$, so it equals $42 + 42 = 84^\circ$. You can check this in triangle $PSR$: $84 + 52 + 44 = 180$.

A.why: This is angle $PQR$, which is also equal to base angle $QPS$. It is a step in the chain, not the angle at $S$.

C.why: You assumed $PS$ bisects angle $QPR$, which gives $47 + 42$. The question never says that. The given condition is $QS = PS$.

D.why: This is angle $PSQ$, the interior angle of triangle $PQS$ at $S$. Angle $PSR$ is the supplementary angle on the other side of $PS$.

items.subtype_name: Multi-step angle chase through a composite figure
items.stimulus: An ornithologist models a flight path with triangle $ABC$. Point $A$ lies on line $\ell$, and points $B$ and $C$ lie on line $m$, with $B$ to the left of $C$. Line $\ell$ is parallel to line $m$. Point $P$ lies on $\ell$ to the left of $A$, point $Q$ lies on $\ell$ to the right of $A$, and point $D$ lies on $m$ to the right of $C$. The measure of angle $PAB$ is $(4x)^\circ$, the measure of angle $BAC$ is $(2x)^\circ$, and the measure of angle $CAQ$ is $(3x + 5)^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ACD$?
items.explanation: The three angles at $A$ lie along line $\ell$, so $4x + 2x + (3x + 5) = 180$. Then $9x = 175$ and $x = \frac{175}{9}$. Angle $ACB$ is the alternate interior angle to angle $CAQ$, so it measures $3\left(\frac{175}{9}\right) + 5 = \frac{190}{3}$ degrees. Angle $ACD$ forms a linear pair with angle $ACB$, so it measures $180 - \frac{190}{3} = \frac{350}{3}$ degrees.

A.why: This is the value of $x$, not an angle measure. You stopped before substituting it into any angle.

B.why: This is angle $ACB$, the interior angle of the triangle at $C$. Angle $ACD$ is the exterior angle beside it, so you still need to subtract from 180.

C.why: This is $4x$, which is angle $PAB$ and also its alternate interior partner, angle $ABC$. It is at vertex $B$, not at $C$.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Food regulators in several countries permit a "reduced fat" label on any product containing at least 25 percent less fat than its standard version. The rule was meant to steer calorie-conscious shoppers toward lighter foods. Nutrition researcher Ilse Marten notes, however, that manufacturers often restore the flavor lost with the fat by adding sugar or starch, so that many labeled products contain nearly as many calories as the originals. Consequently, the label may ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: persuade most shoppers that added sugar is a healthier ingredient than fat is.
lead shoppers to buy products with more calories than the standard versions contain.
steer shoppers who use it to cut calories toward foods that barely help them do so.
lead shoppers who ignore nutrition labels to eat more fat than they did before.
items.explanation: The label's goal is to help calorie-conscious shoppers, but the products it marks have nearly as many calories as the originals. The unintended effect lands on the group the rule was meant to help: the shoppers who trust the label get foods that do little to lower their calories.

A.why: You added a belief the passage never mentions. Nothing suggests shoppers decide sugar is healthier, and "most" is a strength the text can't support.

B.why: You fell for strength creep. The passage says "nearly as many" calories, not more. The labeled products come close to the originals but are never said to exceed them.

D.why: You pinned the harm on the wrong group. The rule was aimed at shoppers who read labels, and the passage says nothing about people who ignore them or about how much fat they eat.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Baroque keyboard scores often look sparse: a single bass line with a few numerals written beneath it. Early modern students of the repertoire took this sparseness as a sign that the pieces were easy to play. Musicologist Tomás Ruelas argues the reverse. The numerals, he shows, told performers which harmonies to improvise in real time above the bass, a skill that took years of training to master. There is thus a disparity between ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: how little of the music the page records and how much the performer was expected to supply.
how easy the pieces were to play and how complicated their notation looked.
how hard the pieces were to perform and how long improvisation took to learn.
the harmonies composers intended and the harmonies performers chose to play.
items.explanation: The two sides are a page that records very little (a bass line and numerals) and a performer who must improvise full harmonies on top of it. The disparity is between what is written down and what the player has to provide.

B.why: You reversed the contrast. The notation looks simple and the playing is hard, not the other way around.

C.why: You paired two things from the same side. Hard performance and long training both describe the demanding half, so the simple-looking notation is missing and no disparity is named.

D.why: You invented a conflict. The passage never says performers departed from what composers intended. It says the numerals told them which harmonies to improvise.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Earthen levees are built along rivers to reduce the damage floods cause to nearby communities. Hydrologists have long observed, however, that land behind a new levee tends to attract homes and businesses, since it is now regarded as safe. Each levee is designed to withstand floods only up to a specified size, and larger floods, though rare, still occur. Consequently, a levee may ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: fail during the ordinary floods that it was specifically designed to hold back.
shift the floods it prevents upstream onto communities located farther downstream.
protect the new homes and businesses behind it from most of the river's floods.
increase the amount of property exposed to floods larger than it can withstand.
items.explanation: The levee is meant to reduce flood damage, but it draws new building onto land that is still at risk from rare, larger floods. So it can increase the amount of property those big floods would damage, which is the opposite of its goal.

A.why: You ignored the design limit. The passage says levees hold up to their specified size. The risk comes from rarer, larger floods, not ordinary ones.

B.why: You added an extra step. Downstream effects may be real in some places, but the passage never mentions them. Its argument is entirely about building behind the levee.

C.why: You stated only one side of the tension. Protection from most floods is the levee's intended benefit. The question asks what follows from the gap between that safety and the rare large flood.

items.subtype_name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
items.stimulus: Nineteenth-century collectors who transcribed oral folktales saw themselves as rescuing a tradition from disappearance. Folklorist Maren Aalto observes that oral tales had survived precisely by changing, since each teller adapted plot and detail to the audience at hand. Once a printed version circulated in a region, however, villagers increasingly treated it as the correct telling and corrected storytellers who departed from it. The unintended effect of the collectors' work was thus to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: preserve tales that would otherwise have been forgotten within a generation.
weaken the very variability that had allowed the tradition to survive.
make villagers lose interest in hearing tales performed by local storytellers.
encourage tellers to adapt printed tales more freely to suit their audiences.
items.explanation: The collectors wanted to keep the tradition alive, and Aalto says it survived by varying. Print made one version the "correct" one and discouraged variation, so the collectors undermined the thing that had kept the tradition going.

A.why: You gave the intended goal, not the unintended effect. Preservation is what the collectors hoped for, and "within a generation" is a claim the passage never makes.

C.why: You went beyond the text. Villagers kept listening closely enough to correct tellers, so nothing shows they lost interest.

D.why: You reversed the effect. Villagers corrected tellers who departed from the printed version, which discouraged free adaptation.
